entries.title: All-DMV High School Volleyball Players of Week 6
entries.summary: This week’s group features outside hitters from West Springfield and Holy Cross, and a middle blocker from Poolesville.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

This week’s volleyball standouts terrorized opponents across the D.C. area. In another competitive week of local play, here are three players who excelled:

Megan Elder, Junior, Middle Blocker, Poolesville

When the Falcons need a spark, they turn to their star middle blocker. Elder has provided an array of highlight plays for Poolesville amid its 5-2 start — the junior Fairfield commit is known for spiking home thunderous kills and blocks at the net for coach Steve Lostoski’s team.

Through Poolesville’s first seven matches, Elder swung at an efficient .539 clip. She amassed 18 kills in a win over Northwood last week and is already up to 127 kills on the season.

“When [Elder] comes in and she gets one of those kills … the crowd goes crazy, the gym goes crazy, and it just seems to lift everyone up,” Lostoski said. “It just energizes everybody.”

Milena Kibret, Senior, Outside Hitter, West Springfield

We’ve reached the middle of October, and West Springfield has yet to drop a set. The defending Virginia Class 6 champion has breezed through its regular-season schedule with a stifling defense and dominant offense. Kibret has produced on both sides at outside hitter: Last week, the NYU commit posted a .471 hitting percentage in wins over Robinson and C.G. Woodson.

“She’s got a heavy, hard arm swing on the ball,” West Springfield coach Stephanie Noriega said. “She’s the kid where you’d leave the gym and think ‘Wow, that No. 7, I wish she was on my team.’”

Emme Wolfe, Junior, Outside Hitter, Holy Cross

Wolfe provides a consistent offensive threat at the outside hitter position for coach Dave Geiser’s Tartans. The high-flying junior has already eclipsed 200 kills on the season, 18 of which came in a 3-1 victory over defending Maryland 4A state champion Broadneck last week. The Houston commit then added 14 more against Jackson-Reed two days later. Holy Cross hasn’t lost since starting the season 1-2 and is riding high with the Washington Catholic Athletic Conference playoffs looming.

“She’s always been a great hitter and a really strong server,” Geiser said. “She’s really passing well in the serve-receive, and then her blocking has really come along.”

entries.title: Byron Donalds Sees Black Voters As Key — Even If the GOP Doesn’t
entries.summary: “You know how you buy some stuff, put it in the garage and forget that it’s there? That’s where the effort is at,” a Black GOP strategist said of the national party’s outreach.
entries.content:
MIAMI — In a bright yellow room, filled with art from the Dominican Republic alongside traditional African masks, Rep. Byron Donalds held court with about two dozen South Florida local politicians, business and community leaders — mostly men, nearly all Black — many of whom identified as Democrats.

Donalds entered the closed-door event where a warm but weary room of people were ready to listen to the Republican lawmaker’s political pitch as he runs for governor. Those who advocated on his behalf said it was finally their chance, as Black people, to have a seat at the table of power in Florida. The skeptical attendees grilled the three-term congressman about his support for President Donald Trump ending temporary protected status for Haitian immigrants, diversity policies and the rising cost of health care.

The lawmaker was kind but unapologetic in his responses. “What you will get from me is candor,” he told the room. “What I ask from you is the same.”

He secured at least a half-dozen endorsements at that event. The new supporters would now back one of the nation’s most prominent conservatives … who just happens to be Black.

endorsement house1.jpg (3024x4032, AR: 0.75)But during multiple interviews with The Washington Sun, Donalds was reluctant to discuss his own Blackness.

“The vast majority of the time, I go out of my way to change the subject,” Donalds said, wearing his signature black suit with a blue tie. “Because I think [the election] has to be about ideas. I think it has to be about vision.”

It’s a quandary Black politicians on both sides of the aisle have faced for years: Does centering their race alienate voters outside of it? And is that amplified for Donalds, who is a Black man in a Republican Party that has decimated diversity policies across the country to appeal to its largely white base who say they are overlooked and forgotten?

The son of a Panamanian American and Jamaican American must confront those reservations as he scales up his effort to court Black Floridians. But the national Republican Party doesn’t appear to share that desire. Nearly a dozen GOP operatives, lawmakers and local elected officials told The Sun they see a contraction in Republican coalition efforts nationwide to maintain the number of Black voters who defected from the Democratic Party in 2024 to vote for Trump.

“You know how you buy some stuff, put it in the garage and forget that it’s there? That’s where the effort is at,” a Black GOP strategist told The Sun, describing the Republican Party’s efforts to win the support of Black voters. The operative, like others in this story, spoke on the condition of anonymity to speak freely without fear of the party’s retribution.

The Frederick Douglass Freedom Alliance pitched the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) and the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) in early spring on a canvassing and messaging plan to target Black voters for nearly a half-dozen races in the midterm elections, according to three people familiar with the events. The NRSC and NRCC both rejected the pitch. Individual GOP campaigns also rejected or didn’t respond to similar pitches from other Black grassroots groups, the sources said.

"President Trump's 2024 strategy proved intentional, relationship driven engagement in black and brown communities works. Now, the Republican Party needs to trust that model, invest in it, and stick with it,” Troy Rolling, the president and CEO of the Frederick Douglass Freedom Alliance, said in a statement to The Sun.

But the lack of action was disappointing but not inherently surprising, according to a second Black GOP operative with knowledge of the pitch, given the challenges the Republican Party is facing less than four weeks before Election Day.

“I don't think the expectation is that we're gonna have a large amount of Black folks coming out to support us because we can't even get the white folks to support us,” the operative said.

The NRCC said the GOP has been working to “earn the trust of Black voters,” and put the onus back on Democrats.

“House Democrats have taken too many voters for granted, and families across the country want nothing to do with their radical socialist policies that will make life harder,” NRCC spokesperson Mike Marinella said in a statement.

When asked whether the GOP was doing enough nationwide to target Black voters, Donalds demurred: “I think a lot of the party doesn't know how, and I don't think it's that they don't want to. I just think they don't know how.”

The congressman has launched a targeted push to win the support of the Black community, which makes up around 12% of Florida’s more than 13 million voters. The state has voted three times to elect Trump — in 2024, he won the state by 13 percentage points. Donalds, if elected, would be the first Black Republican governor of that state, and the first Black governor elected nationwide in decades.

The campaign has spent upwards of seven figures targeting Black voters in Florida, according to a source familiar with the operations, including at least $1 million on ads focused on the community, the source said. One of those ads, which has not yet debuted, will feature Donalds’ mother talking about how the lawmaker was raised. The Donalds campaign rolled out its first ad targeted at Black voters last week.

Facing off against Democrat David Jolly in a race that has become tighter than expected, Donalds wants to pick up votes from more Democrats, and his goal is to get more Black votes than any previous Republican gubernatorial nominee in Florida.

“I want all the Black vote because I want everybody's vote,” Donalds told The Sun during a car ride from one event to the next. Outgoing Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis secured 15% of the Black vote in his 2015 gubernatorial race but failed to meet that threshold when he was reelected in 2023. Now Donalds says he wants to beat it. “I think if I was just gonna just throw it on the table, I think north of 20 [percent].”

Donalds is barnstorming Black businesses, barbershops and churches. He’s meeting with key stakeholders from the large diaspora of Black people in Florida, including those of Caribbean descent like his parents.

“To do some of this, we've had to build new muscle that typically is not built in Republican campaigns,” Donalds said.

The larger GOP’s lack of infrastructure and intentionality nationwide to appeal to Black voters represents a missed opportunity to some who hoped that the party could capitalize on the gains from the last presidential election and crystallize a generational shift of key voters away from the Democratic Party. Trump received 15% of the Black vote nationally, according to Pew Research, in a race against Vice President Kamala Harris, who was running to become the first Black female president. The numbers were largely fueled by Black men, with 21% of the voting bloc supporting Trump. 

The 2024 Trump campaign, along with allied super PACs, spent millions to win the support of Black men. Trump visited barbershops. He appeared with prominent (if not older) members of the Black community. And his campaign placed ads where it believed Black men were watching. From a national standpoint, operatives told The Sun, that isn’t happening during this election cycle.

“Black men gave Republicans an opportunity mostly because of the economic concerns that were very valid and legitimate, and yet we didn't do anything to shore up those concerns," a prominent Black Republican strategist told The Sun, blaming the White House for the absence of any policy that addressed Black voters' concerns.

The Black unemployment rate jumped a full percentage point to 7% since last year, nearly double the unemployment rate for white people. And the administration’s anti-DEI policies forced hundreds of thousands of Black women out of their jobs, MS NOW reported.

The Education Department announced a one-time injection of nearly $175 million to strengthen Historically Black Colleges and Universities in September. While the announcement appeared on the agency’s website, no official acknowledgement came from the White House. There was no Oval Office event or even a mention of it in any of Trump’s many Truth Social posts. The White House circulated a paper statement celebrating HBCUs generally a day before the Education Department’s announcement. Multiple people suggested to The Sun that the White House lacks a communicator who values that type of news, nor does it want to appear to be pushing DEI policies close to the midterms.

“So Black men are looking at us, and they're saying, ‘Nothing really changed for me. There's not a damn thing I can point to as tangible to say my life has gotten better,’” the strategist said.

When asked why it didn’t formally announce the HBCU money or if Trump plans to propose specific policy geared toward Black Americans, the White House said, “President Trump has done more for Black Americans than any other President in recent history.”

“From investing more than $80 billion into low-income census tract Opportunity Zones, driving violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century, passing the largest middle-class tax cuts in American history, putting American children on a path toward generational wealth through Trump Accounts, advancing criminal justice reform, and increasing his historic HBCU funding by an additional $174 million dollars in September 2026, President Trump will never stop fighting to make everyday life better and more affordable for Americans,” White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said in a statement.

Strategists credit Rep. John James, another Black Republican who’s running for governor in Michigan, for his campaign focused in part on turning out the Black vote for the party. He recently appeared with the popular Detroit rapper 42 Dugg. The duo discussed James’ vision, and the congressman joined the rapper onstage at a concert wearing fresh white Air Force One Nike sneakers. Dugg took down the video after facing backlash, according to two sources familiar with his thinking, and privately complained that appearing with James hurt his reputation. The video is still up on James’ Facebook.

Many operatives question how much effort Republican Senate candidates like Georgia’s Mike Collins, who is caught up in another Ku Klux Klan-associated scandal, and Michigan’s Mike Rogers are putting into corralling Black voters.

Linda Lee Tarver, a Republican activist in Michigan, has been one of several surrogates accompanying Rogers to meetings with Black stakeholders in the state, including pastors, small business owners and advocates focused on education and housing issues. Tarver said she isn’t seeing a contraction in GOP efforts nationwide to reach Black voters but suggested the party’s messaging could be missing the mark.

“I would push back and say we have great policies. We may not be able to, in some states, communicate them effectively, but our policies are criminal justice reform, reentry, jobs and education and technical trade, all of those are very important. I believe that we're on the right side of the policy. Are our communicators the best? I don't know,” she said.

The Republican National Committee has launched specific programs focused on Black voters in only a handful of states, which all voted for Trump in 2024: Florida, Michigan, North Carolina and Georgia, according to a GOP official. But it’s unclear if that strategy is working.

A September survey from YouGov/Economist found that just 6% of Black voters said they totally approved of Trump’s job in office, while 6% said they strongly approved or somewhat approved.

Florida, By Way of Brooklyn

Donalds, a Brooklyn native who took a bus to Florida for college and then never left, comes off differently in real life than the mudslinger most people see on TV. In front of crowds, he recites facts about the state’s permitting process, a source of pain for the Floridians looking to build or renovate homes, and riffs on access to capital for small businesses, insurance cost reductions and the state’s education system — a purposeful effort to show he can lead.

“I probably would say a Black Republican is a minority in political life. It's not just in the party; it's across all politics,” Donalds said. “Number one, you definitely have to command the issues because everybody wants to have an opinion about your political views, especially on the other side of the aisle. Number two, you really have to be able to weather … every storm. Because people talk about you. They try to talk about your family. They try to talk about your upbringing. A lot of people who don't know you just cast aspersions."

His solutions are rooted in pragmatism and cutting red tape, he said. Attendees who spoke with The Sun after his appearances earlier this month said he was approachable and even charming.

“He was totally different talking to us than some of the things I saw in the past,” said Carlos Rolle, an engineer and business owner from Miami Gardens who met Donalds at a Caribbean restaurant for an intimate group conversation. Rolle, a Bahamian American, went into the conversation undecided. But Donalds has won his vote.

“What I like about him, he's at least trying to do the work. He's not sending a surrogate to do things,” Rolle said. “He knows that a lot of people are gonna shut him out. They won’t want to talk to him, they won’t want to be shown with him in the media. But he’s trying. I believe in effort.”

Part of their discussion centered on whether Donalds was prepared to be his own man and do what’s in the best interest of Florida — even if that runs counter to what any president might want. Rolle said Donalds told them he was. Donalds’ support for Trump undergirded those conversations.
President Donald Trump and Rep. Byron Donalds (5400x3600, AR: 1.50)In 2023, the congressman made a risky bet: He endorsed Trump over DeSantis for the presidential nomination, solidifying him as a MAGA firebrand. Donalds became a face for Trump’s outreach to Black voters during the 2024 election, leading his own series of barbershop events. And since Trump returned to the White House, Donalds has sided with the president on most of his most controversial actions — including immigration enforcement, dismantling DEI initiatives and the Iran war. Donalds is close to Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, and many of her close allies serve as consultants for Donalds’ campaign.

Donalds has been confronted on the campaign trail about his loyalty to the president.

“There's a skepticism. There's no doubt about that,” Donalds said.

Asked if his support of Trump has hurt his efforts to flip Black voters, the congressman was careful: “Yeah, maybe.”

“But again, I was a surrogate for the president,” Donalds added. “I was glad to do it.”

Donalds denied that scrubbing his website of any mention of Trump was meant to put distance between him and a president with a sinking approval rating. His campaign noted that the website shows visitors a pop-up of the president's endorsement.

But it’s an uphill climb for Donalds. A Mason-Dixon survey released this week showed Donalds with a large lead over Jolly but only netting 10% of the Black vote, with 14% still undecided. A poll released this week by YouGov had Donalds at 9% with Black voters.

That tension was evident in some conversations on the trail. Donalds was confronted repeatedly about Trump’s policies that he has either adopted or championed at campaign events.

At a private event in Miami’s Design District, Eric Knowles, the president and CEO of the Miami-Dade Chamber of Commerce, told Donalds: “We know in our community woke meant being aware of what's going on, and it seems like it's been stolen by the left or right or whatever. And again, it's about being awake, and it's like it's taking on this connotation of ‘we are bad because we're woke.’”

Jeffery Daub, a firefighter who attended the event with his wife, left unconvinced.

“He is who he is, and I take him for who he is,” said Daub, who researched Donalds’ positions during his car ride home after the event. “I don't expect him to do anything other than what I see anyone who was associated with Trump doing.”

And while waiting to enter the annual Caribbean Carnival in Tarmac City, Florida, Olivia H. told The Sun she won’t vote for Donalds because he’s a Republican, despite his race.

“I'm poor. I'm Black. I'm a woman. I'm [pro-choice]. I am a daughter of immigrants, so I'm not gonna vote for a party that doesn't reflect the needs of that community,” she said.

As Donalds courts Black votes, it remains an open question whether he can win over white voters in the northern and central parts of Florida who may be reluctant to elect a Black governor.

“It’s about how them white boys in Central Florida feel,” said a worker at the House of Wings, a food truck that catered one of Donalds’ events and who asked not to be named. “That’s the key. It ain't about us.”

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Who’s Your Landlord?
entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Calls for a revamped rental registry, Tom Sietsema on Rose’s Luxury and Thomas Boswell on the Commanders’ calamitous tie.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 8/10. 80 degrees won't be a hit with the pumpkin spice latte crowd, but this sunny, comfortable-humidity day is still plenty nice! Full forecast from Capital Weather.

THE LATEST

So you want to know who owns your rental property? Good luck tracking down an actual human.

D.C. logs who has a stake in the LLCs, nonprofits, co-ops and for-profit corporations that own housing in D.C. online, listing any other properties those “beneficial owners” own. New York City may be the only other jurisdiction in the country that does so.

Because of how the law defines a “person,” sometimes searching that D.C. database just churns up another business entity. Advocates say that is partly why it’s been so challenging to hold bad actors accountable here, and why D.C.’s Department of Buildings is owed almost $87 million for unresolved code violations, The Washington Sun’s Zara Norman reports.

That’s why some are calling for the city to require that a “natural person” be listed, with contact information, alongside each LLC in a public-facing registry. It could help D.C. better perform “clean hands” inspections, advocates say, ensuring that landlords receiving city business don’t owe fines and penalties under a different LLC.

“Our systems are not talking to each other,” Ward 5 council member Zachary Parker told The Sun. “We have a system that essentially allows many landlords to go without enforcement or consequences.”

Not everyone is convinced that another registry is a vehicle for fixing poor housing conditions in the District. At a recent housing committee hearing, dozens of landlords said tenants’ sustained nonpayment of rent and a slow-marching eviction process are preventing them from injecting capital back into their properties.

“Another public registry is the tenant advocacy bureaucracy outdoing itself with another unnecessary burden, and it couldn't come at the worst time,” said Dean Hunter, the CEO of D.C.’s Small Multifamily & Rental Owners Association. “We have a rent payment crisis that has deeply destabilized affordable housing. I believe we're about six months away from a wave of affordable housing foreclosures.”

DEEP DIVE

A federal judge tore into Trump administration lawyers over the removal of some 430 trees — many of them healthy — from East Potomac Park over the weekend without giving her sufficient advance notice, The Sun’s Mara Hoplamazian, Reese Gorman and Todd Ruger report.

The showdown took place during a last-minute, four-hour hearing on Monday where Judge Ana C. Reyes grilled attorneys from the Justice Department, one official from the National Park Service and another from the Interior Department over the administration’s late-Friday notification that it would start clearing more than 500 trees the following day.

Reyes was incredulous that she had been notified so late about the project, despite ongoing litigation related to President Donald Trump’s plans to renovate the East Potomac Park golf course into what many fear would be luxury links that would be out of reach for the general public.

“You did your absolute worst,” she thundered at a DOJ lawyer over his claim that they did their best to notify her of the tree-clearing ahead of time. She also said the government had lost credibility with her, and ordered a senior Interior Department official to appear this week to testify as to what has happened — and “whether or not I’ve been lied to.”

Reyes has forbidden any more work at East Potomac Park through Tuesday afternoon, pending further testimony to determine whether the Trump administration lied to her about its plans. “I am thoroughly unamused right now,” she said.

FROM THE DISTRICT

D.C. has selected a team to build a new $77 million indoor sportsplex alongside the new Commanders stadium at the RFK campus on the east end of Capitol Hill, the Washington Business Journal reports. The sportsplex will sit to the north of the stadium, on a portion of the campus that will be reserved for sports and recreation.

Federal agents searched the D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar yesterday morning as part of a criminal investigation, The Sun’s Elise Foley and Mara Hoplamazian report. It’s a highly unusual move this close to an election.

The Kennedy Center has tapped talent manager Rick Canny to be its new artistic director, WAMU reports. Canny, whose previous clients include ZZ Top and Mötley Crüe drummer Tommy Lee, has been working as a consultant to the storied — and recently beleaguered — arts institution since February 2025.

FROM VIRGINIA

It’s restaurant week in Arlington, which means you can score discounted meals at more than 70 area restaurants through Monday.

FROM MARYLAND

The University of Maryland’s club tennis team has been suspended indefinitely after a Howard University student found racist images in informational materials for a tournament the Maryland team hosted, WUSA9 reports.

FROM THE DINING ROOM

Tom Sietsema, The Sun’s food correspondent, dishes on a hump day deal.

The drill at Rose’s Luxury on the Hill for the past five years — five courses for $133 — isn’t every diner’s jam, even though patrons get to make a few choices on the set-price menu. Memorable as the cooking is, some of us don’t want to commit to that much food, which includes can’t-miss milk bread, a sharable entree and what the menu calls “slightly ridiculously-sized desserts.” True that.

What lured this fan back recently was the news that Rose’s Luxury offers the option of a la carte on Wednesday nights. A recent hump day found me at the counter of the second-floor bar, inhaling the restaurant’s signature pork and lychee salad topped with a little cloud of coconut foam.

“Destroy it to enjoy it,” instructed an attendant. For sure, the best way to eat the $25 assembly is to swirl the contents in the bowl so you can taste the dozen-plus other ingredients, including mint, garlic chips, shaved red onion, peanut and pickled habanero. Zing went the strings of my heart.

Next up was bucatini tossed with a rich sungold tomato sauce and priced at $19. Cooked to retain some bite, the subtly sweet pasta trumpets cracked pepper, fresh basil and cheese. The dishes were preceded by the elegant Rose is Luxury: rye whiskey, lemon juice and rose-flavored simple syrup.

Owner Aaron Silverman says the restaurant makes about $30 less per person when it offers a la carte, an idea introduced in February, and tries to offset the difference with greater turnover of tables. Acknowledging that people are watching their dining budgets more closely these days, he’s open to expanding the deal to other days of the week. Yes, please!

Turns out the playful restaurant just celebrated 13 years, prompting a staffer to congratulate his boss with “Happy bar mitzvah!”

WHAT YOU GET WITH A FIREPLACE

261008-living-space-brentwood-place-ak (2048x1365, AR: 1.50)This week’s real estate column looks at what buyers can get for less than $1 million with a wood-burning fireplace.

Where is this house listed? Click on your guess to see the answer:

  1. Maryland
  2. Virginia
  3. D.C.

SPORTS

Long before the disastrous, somewhat inexplicable conclusion to the Commanders’ Week 5 tie with the Giants, Washington’s defense collapsed. After stifling New York for much of the afternoon, the unit surrendered three touchdowns on three straight possessions to squander a 14-point lead. So, what happened? The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson studied the game tape to find out.

The Sun’s Thomas Boswell believes Sunday’s game-ending snafu was the worst he’s seen in his 70 years following Washington’s football team. “The Commanders had not one but two absolute imperatives: Make sure you get off a field goal attempt, and run off as much time as you (safely) can before that kick in case you miss,” he writes. “Turns out that, even in this most generous of evaluations, the Commanders couldn’t walk and chew gum at the same time.”

What to Watch Today

NHL: Capitals at Hurricanes, 6:45 p.m. (Monumental)

Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com. Finally, yesterday’s trivia answer was B) 1964. That was the first presidential election that included D.C. voters. A special shout-out to Donna Fletcher, who answered first.

entries.title: Morning Sun: MAGA’s Big Tent Shrinks
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Republicans have a Black voter problem (again). The state of things in Alaska. A gambling scoop. Katie Zacharia’s first briefing. And a crackdown on American voters who haven’t resided in the U.S. 

THE LATEST

Not long ago, MAGA’s inroads with Black voters were a defining storyline of a movement that sought to remake the Republican Party. But three weeks before Election Day, that excitement has faded into frustration. The Washington Sun’s Jasmine Wright took a deep dive into where things stand now with this unlikely coalition.

Enter Rep. Byron Donalds, Florida’s GOP gubernatorial candidate, who is spending more than $1 million to target Black voters in his state. He hopes to build on Trump’s 2024 numbers with Black voters — he wants “north of 20 [percent]” of Black votes in his state, he told Jasmine recently in Florida.

The problem: He has to start basically from square one. Nearly a dozen GOP operatives, lawmakers and local elected officials told Jasmine that the mainstream GOP failed to maintain the support of the 15% of Black voters Trump won in 2024.

“You know how you buy some stuff, put it in the garage and forget that it’s there? That’s where the effort is at,” a Black Republican strategist told her.

One anecdote: The Frederick Douglass Freedom Alliance pitched the National Republican Senatorial Committee and the National Republican Congressional Committee in early spring on a canvassing and messaging plan to target Black voters for nearly a half-dozen races in the midterm elections, Jasmine reports. Both committees rejected the pitch.

When asked whether the Republican Party is doing enough nationwide to target Black voters, Donalds demurred: “I think a lot of the party doesn't know how, and I don't think it's that they don't want to. I just think they don't know how.”

More: Trump’s Taxpayer-Funded Ads Kept Running After a Court Ordered Him to Stop • Republican-Aligned Super PAC Buys Ads in the Wrong Portland • Trump Says He Had ‘Nothing to Do With’ the Raid on Ilhan Omar’s Home

FROM ALASKA

What is Trump going to find when he visits the state today? Our Alex Roarty just got back from Alaska and has a report on the state of the Senate race, just as the president hits the ground to stump for his party.

A senior member of Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan’s campaign told Alex they believed that, had the election been held at the start of October, the senator would have lost. But they said the past two weeks have bolstered Sullivan enough that if the election were held now, they believe he would win.

Democrats still feel very good about Mary Peltola’s chances, especially when the state’s ranked-choice voting system is factored in. In past races, many GOP-aligned voters only ranked their top candidate and left the rest of the ballot blank. That could cost Sullivan thousands of votes and swing the election. “That’s frustrating, right?” he told Alex.

FROM THE FTC

Scoop: The feds are looking into sportsbetting. Federal Trade Commission officials are probing the $167 billion online sports gambling industry, The Sun’s Jeff Stein is first to report. While the evaluation is in its early stages, sources said it’s likely to focus on allegations of deceptive and misleading ads from online sportsbooks such as FanDuel and DraftKings. Both companies have denied wrongdoing.

FROM THE WHITE HOUSE

What to expect in the briefing room: New press secretary Katie Zacharia is slated to hold her first press briefing at 9:30 a.m. The Sun's Ben T.N. Mause said he'll be watching for hostility at the podium: “Multiple people have told me she's cool behind the scenes. But how's she going to react to a tough question? And will she maintain the status quo, or will she raise or lower the level of antagonism with the press?”

NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

The war on “never resided” voters. Trump administration officials removed an option to request a ballot for American citizens abroad who have never lived full time in the U.S. — children of diplomats or military service members, for example. Reporting for The Sun, Rebecca Ritzel takes a close look at a broad effort to restrict this kind of absentee voting that includes the Pentagon and the Republican National Committee.

entries.title: The FTC Is Beginning to Probe the Sports Gambling Industry
entries.summary: Preliminary discussions at the Federal Trade Commission come despite the Trump administration’s embrace of the booming industry.
entries.content:
Officials at the Federal Trade Commission are probing the $167 billion online sports gambling industry, which has been celebrated by the White House but faces mounting skepticism from some conservative activists.

The FTC’s interest in online sports gambling is expected to focus on online sportsbooks such as FanDuel and DraftKings — probably on allegations of deceptive and misleading advertisements, three sources familiar with the matter said. Both political and career staffers at the agency have been involved in reviewing online sports books, the sources said, though the evaluation is in its early stages.

The review, which has not been previously reported, is not expected to include the “prediction markets” such as Kalshi and Polymarket.

Online sports betting has exploded since the Supreme Court struck down a federal ban in 2018. About half of men age 18 to 49 have an active account with an online sportsbook, according to a February poll by the Siena Research Institute and St. Bonaventure University’s Jandoli School of Communication. Researchers have documented increases in suicide, hospitalizations and bankruptices among users. These adverse effects are expected to be part of the agency’s review, one of the sources said.

The Trump administration has so far taken a hands-off approach with the industry, and the White House even promoted an advertisement for Stake, which offers sports betting, during the UFC event held on the South Lawn this summer. But the administration is facing a growing chorus of social conservatives alarmed by its effect on young men.

While the FTC’s review remains preliminary, any investigation of the sports books would have major consequences for an industry that now has tens of millions of active users. Online sports gambling companies have fiercely resisted regulatory efforts, and they have been embraced by both Democratic and Republican officials for providing large amounts of tax revenue and political donations.

But there are some signs the tides are changing. Jon Schweppe, a former FTC senior policy adviser under Trump-appointed FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, has argued it is "time to put the online sportsbooks in the hot seat," comparing them to Big Tobacco, Big Tech and Big Pharma.

“They’re isolating specific customers who are problem gamblers and psychologically manipulating them to part with as much money as possible,” said Schweppe, who is now part of the American Principles Project, a right-leaning organization. “I don’t think there’s an appetite for a federal ban on sports gambling, but we should protect consumers from certain types of predatory behavior.”

The New York Times reported last month that DraftKings targets losing bettors with promotions that encourage more gambling, citing interviews with more than 40 employees. FanDuel has faced similar accusations, including a recent charge that it delivered a personalized video of MLB star Bryce Harper to a gambler who was $1.5 million in debt.

One advocacy group claims that in sports betting, 86% of revenue comes from 5% of players.

Both companies have denied wrongdoing. A spokesman for DraftKings said the FTC has not sent it a Civil Investigative Demand, a kind of subpoena issued by the agency. FanDuel declined to comment, as did a spokesperson for the FTC.

Joe Maloney, the president of the Sports Betting Alliance, told The Sun that the Responsible Online Gaming Association's code of conduct "represents a commitment by ROGA’s members to uphold a set of consistent marketing standards that advances consumer protection." He also pointed to Nielsen Ad Intel research commissioned by the American Gaming Association that found the sportsbooks accounted for 0.8% of spending on television commercials in 2024, while alcohol ads accounted for 1.4%.

Maloney also strongly pushed back on claims that online sports gambling contributed to increases in suicide, hospitalization, and poor financial outcomes. He pointed to a study by the centrist Progressive Policy Institute that found that legalized sports betting "has not produced the widespread financial fallout that critics feared." That study found credit scores in states with legal sports betting have been in line with national trends.

One of the sources familiar with the matter said a growing number of younger Republicans have become acutely aware of the danger posed by sports gambling.

"There's a real generational divide on this: A lot of the older officials don't get what the big deal is," they said. "But younger appointees really get it. They get that the sports betting enterprise now is fundamentally different and wiping out entire families."

Experts are divided on whether prediction markets such as Polymarket and Kalshi should be excluded from an FTC probe of sports betting. While those platforms allow users to win money by guessing the outcome of games, they have argued that they do not amount to gambling and are “event contracts” similar to options trading on the stock market.

The prediction markets say the price of sports trades on their platforms is set by the public, reducing the incentive for misleading promotions, and argue that sportsbooks make money only when the house wins, creating an incentive to hook addictive gamblers. Complicating the landscape, however, are newer prediction markets hosted by sportsbetting companies.

Others have been skeptical of those claims. Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut) has announced legislation to police platforms like Kalshi, arguing the prediction markets offer “services that are substantially the same as betting, wagering, gambling and sports gambling.”

In June, The Wall Street Journal reported that Polymarket had flooded social media with deceptive videos by paid creators who appear to be getting rich on the platform, when none of the winnings were real.

Monica Vaca, a consumer protection attorney who practiced for more than two decades at the FTC, said the allegations fall squarely within the agency's wheelhouse and would justify opening an investigation of all the platforms involved. The FTC could use its subpoena authority and civil investigative demands to get information from the companies and find out what happened.

“This has been the bread-and-butter work of the agency for decades,” Vaca said. “The FTC has an extremely broad jurisdiction over the marketplace.”

entries.title: The Trump Administration’s Quiet Crackdown on ‘Never-Resided’ Voters
entries.summary: More than three dozen states allow Americans who have never lived in the United States to vote, but the Department of Defense and the RNC are trying to put an end to the practice.
entries.content:
The Trump administration and the Republican National Committee have quietly launched an offensive against a small but potentially important group of voters: Americans who have never lived in the United States.

“Never residents” or “never-resided” voters — the children of Americans abroad — are eligible for passports and must file taxes. In 37 states, plus the District of Columbia, they can vote in federal elections (and sometimes state and local races) wherever an American parent last lived.

According to a 2017 report published by the Federal Voting Assistance Program, 11,590 never-resided Americans were registered to vote as of 2016. Experts say that number has likely swelled in the last decade along with the overall overseas voter count, with higher per-capita numbers in states like Alaska and Michigan.

The RNC is now arguing in court that those laws are illegal and that Americans who have never established residency in the United States should not be allowed to vote in the midterms. Since 2024, the RNC has filed lawsuits challenging those rights in eight states. In June, a North Carolina judge became the first to rule in favor of the RNC.

“Enforcing citizenship and residency requirements isn’t disenfranchisement — it’s following the law,” RNC spokesperson Ally Triolo said in a statement to The Washington Sun.

The RNC says these suits don’t impact “military members or overseas voters who previously lived in a state, both of whom remain legally eligible to vote under state and federal law.”

Several of the pending cases were brought by Restoring Integrity and Trust in Elections, a conservative political action committee. Lawyers for the group argue that because overseas voters — including members of the military — register as Democrats at higher rates than domestic voters, allowing never-resident Americans to vote creates a “state-imposed disadvantage” for Republican candidates.

The Department of Defense, which is congressionally mandated to support all overseas and military voting, meanwhile, has taken the position that all never-residents should be ineligible to vote. In August, the Pentagon quietly removed all references to never-resided voters from key elections materials, including a form used by overseas voters to register and request ballots. The Federal Voting Assistance Guide was suddenly taken offline in August and republished without more than 20 pages of guidance for never-resided voters.

On Oct. 1, the Democratic National Committee sued the Department of Defense and the Office of Management and Budget on behalf of never-resided voters, arguing that the DoD had declared “‘a false ‘emergency’ to alter voter-registration materials without notice and comment in an effort to disenfranchise eligible American citizens.”

In the suit, the DNC notes that prior to Sept. 1, the Federal Post Card Application included a line allowing citizens to check, “I am a U.S. citizen living outside the country, and I have never lived in the United States.’”

Sean O’Keefe, the Pentagon’s deputy under secretary for personnel and readiness, wrote in his Aug. 13 letter to OMB that people “who have never resided in the United States are not within the class of voters” covered by the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act, a 1986 law that standardized military and overseas voting procedures.

OMB granted O’Keefe’s “emergency” request because there was “insufficient time” before the federal election to follow normal procedures.

Martha McDevitt-Pugh, international chair of Democrats Abroad, said the changes followed a frustrating summer for overseas voters, when the Federal Voting Assistance Program website, the online voting resource chartered by Congress and run by the Pentagon, was plagued by broken links and “temporarily unavailable” pages.

“We use that website extensively,” McDevitt-Pugh said.

According to FVAP’s 2024 report to Congress, there are approximately 2.2 million voting-age citizens living abroad. Federal law requires overseas ballots to be mailed by Sept. 19. Because so many states cleaned out voter rolls over the last two years, Democrats Abroad recommended that overseas voters resubmit their applications before the midterms. Many of them were trying to do that in August, when the FVAP website was down.

In a statement to The Washington Sun, a Pentagon spokesperson characterized the FVAP issues as a “routine update” that would “actively protect voting rights and eliminate voter confusion.”

“This includes updated online guidance on August 31 that clarifies instructions and voter eligibility requirements regarding the Federal Post Card Application,” the spokesperson said.

The DNC, Democrats Abroad and voting rights advocates argue those changes are illegal and that never-residents are being discriminated against because of “perceived political preferences,” according to the DNC lawsuit. They warn that there could be chaos in especially close races where overseas ballots that are counted after Election Day could determine the outcome.

“We’re concerned for every voter having their right to vote and having that right be treated as it should be treated and counted,” McDevitt-Pugh said.

Valencia Richardson, a senior legal counsel at the nonpartisan Campaign Legal Center and a former Fulbright scholar who has voted from abroad, pointed out that even when civilians move overseas, they often do so “in service to the United States.” The population includes many diplomats and military contractors whose children turn 18 before ever living in their parents’ home country.

“I like to call them not-yet-resided voters,” McDevitt-Pugh said, pointing out that many Americans who first cast ballots as “never resided” end up moving to the U.S. at some point.

That fluidity is one reason it’s impossible to know how many voters are potentially being disenfranchised by the changes, said Amanda Klekowski von Koppenfels, a scholar at the University of Kent who studies the American diaspora and voting patterns. She raised two children in Brussels, both of whom cast never-resided ballots in 2020 but have since lived in the United States.

Klekowski von Koppenfels pointed out that while UOCAVA, the law that standardized overseas voting, did not explicitly mention never-resided Americans, the follow-up 2010 Uniform Military and Overseas Voters Act (UMOVA) does. That act brought overseas voting into the internet age and encouraged, but did not require, all states to extend federal voting rights to never-resided Americans.

“These are U.S. citizens who are required to file taxes and when applicable, register for the draft,” Klekowski von Koppenfels said. Challenges to their voting rights amount to “taxation without representation,” she said.

North Carolina used UMOVA as the basis for its own military and overseas voting bill, which passed unanimously in 2011. It only came under scrutiny in 2024, when a Republican candidate for state Supreme Court lost by a narrow margin and challenged all overseas ballots.The RNC subsequently sued to eliminate never-resided voting rights in the state and won.

“This is a clear win for fair and lawful elections,” RNC Chair Joe Gruters said in a news release touting the ruling. “The court upheld the North Carolina Constitution and made clear that only North Carolina residents can vote in the state. The RNC will keep fighting to ensure only eligible citizens can vote."

The DNC did not appeal, and it declined to comment on the ruling. Never-resided voting has been upheld in several other states where the RNC has sued, including Nebraska and Michigan. In both of those states, the RNC has appealed.

Challenges also are pending in Arizona, Colorado, Nevada, New Jersey and Virginia.

“The DNC is fighting to ensure American citizens are able to participate in our democracy no matter where they are in the world and hold Trump accountable when they cast their ballot,” Dan Freeman, the DNC’s litigation director, said in a statement.

Overseas ballots typically are counted after Election Day. In 2024, Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) won by 19,006 votes — a nailbiter election in which the state tabulated more than 21,000 votes from abroad, though the counts do not distinguish between overseas military ballots and other citizens who live abroad.

The Washington Sun queried the secretaries of state in three swing states that allow never-resided voting: Alaska, Maine and Michigan. In all three, elections officials pledged to count all overseas ballots, regardless of whether the voters used the August or September versions of the postcard registration form.

“We believe every United States citizen, including those living abroad, has the right to vote in federal elections, and we will do everything in our power to protect the rights of every eligible voter to participate in our democracy,” Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said.

entries.title: This Is Why Trump Is Going to Alaska
entries.summary: Republicans have dominated Alaska for years. But there are distinct issues roiling the state’s races now.
entries.content:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska — President Donald Trump will campaign in Alaska on Tuesday, hoping to boost Republican candidates in a state he won by 13 percentage points in 2024. He has said — repeatedly — that voters should “pretend” he’s on the ballot.

But some Alaska Republicans are happy to remind the public that, actually, Trump isn’t up for reelection this year.

“The president is not on the ballot,” Republican Rep. Nick Begich told The Washington Sun in an interview here last week. “I am. Sen. Sullivan is.”

Asked about the president’s request that GOP voters act like he’s on the ballot, the congressman demurred.

“Republicans should act like he is,” Begich said. “But at the end of the day, his name does not literally appear on the ballot.”

Trump’s visit this week underscores how much is now at stake in Alaska for both the president’s political legacy and his party’s chances of holding onto control of the Senate. Democrats need to gain a net of four Senate seats this year to win a majority, and strategists in both parties view Alaska as a potential tipping-point state in that battle.

Interviews on the ground here make clear just how competitive the state has become, showcasing the vulnerabilities Republicans have in seats they’ve long controlled.

Begich said in the interview that he thought no president had done more for Alaska than Trump thanks to his administration’s priority on natural resource development. And he said he thought the popularity of the administration’s policies was evident in the fact that, although Trump’s approval rating is low, Republicans were performing much better on the generic congressional ballot.

Still, as he is across the map this election, Trump is a drag on Republican candidates in Alaska. The average cost of gasoline is above $5 a gallon and the cost of diesel — which many rural communities purchase before winter as heating fuel — is through the roof.

The president’s tariffs on many foreign goods are also seen as especially harmful, in part because of the state’s long border with Canada.

“People are exhausted by Trump’s shenanigans,” said Joelle Hall, emeritus president of the Alaska AFL-CIO. “They're exhausted by this war. They're exhausted by all the things that are running down upon them, and they just want to change. This feels like a change election.”

Don’t Believe the Polls? 

Republicans and Democrats each dismiss recent public polling that shows Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, Alaska’s former at-large House member, vaulting ahead of Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, insisting the race is neck and neck.

“I don’t think she is 7 points ahead,” former Democratic Sen. Mark Begich told The Sun. “I think it’s more like she’s a couple of points ahead. And the thing about Alaska — if you’re a Democratic candidate and you’re going into the final days and you’re two points ahead, you’re probably tied.”

A New York Times/Siena University survey conducted mostly in September found Peltola with a 7-point lead over Sullivan. It was the second such survey that month to find Peltola with a significant edge, following one from the AARP.

Other surveys have found a tighter race, with the former Democratic congresswoman still holding a small lead.

But Republicans and even some Democrats say they believe Sullivan has made up ground in recent weeks thanks to increased engagement from conservative voters, who had previously expressed little interest in the upcoming election. Republican voters, in other words, are starting to come home.

“We're seeing rising levels of enthusiasm showing up in both internal and publicly released polling data among the Republican and conservative independent base in Alaska,” Nick Begich said in the interview.

One senior Sullivan campaign official, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said they believed that had the election been held at the start of October, the senator would have lost. But the official believed that the last two weeks had bolstered Sullivan enough that if the election were held now, he would win.

Most Alaska Democrats are still confident that Peltola has a small but real edge in the race. A new survey released this week showed the Democratic candidate with a 2-point edge over Sullivan in the fourth round of tabulation.

Ballot Issues

One reason Democrats still think the former congresswoman will win: Alaska’s unusual ranked-choice, top-four ballot system.

It’s not an exaggeration to say that the victor of this Senate race could come down to how a few thousand Republican voters navigate the ballot — something they have not traditionally been very adept at doing.

November’s ballot will include four names. And in a blow to the incumbent senator, one of the other listed candidates is also a Republican, Gerald Heikes, while a second shares the senator’s first and last name, Daniel J. Sullivan.

In a ranked-choice system, Republican voters could either rank the other Sullivan or Heikes first and still list the senator as a second option, which would effectively be the same as ranking him as their top choice in the second or third rounds of tabulation. (Votes are reallocated each round until one candidate obtains a majority.)

But the problem — one that Sen. Dan Sullivan’s campaign is keenly aware of — is that many GOP-aligned voters only rank their top candidate and leave the rest of the ballot blank, even if they would prefer Sullivan to a Democrat like Peltola.

That could cost the senator thousands of votes and swing the election to Peltola — an outcome Republicans bluntly acknowledge is possible.

“That’s frustrating, right?” the incumbent Republican told The Sun in an interview last week, pointing in particular to the other Dan Sullivan. “If he gets 2 or 3% of the vote because people make mistakes, in a close race that could be the difference.”

The senator, speaking from a local Veterans of Foreign Wars hall here at a campaign event, said he was especially frustrated after speaking at a senior center earlier in the day, where he found continued uncertainty about the ballot situation with less than a month to go before Election Day.

“The seniors are confused,” he said.

Sullivan called the presence of the other Sullivan a plot by Democrats to deceive Alaska voters (Daniel J. Sullivan has said he did not coordinate with Democrats and was simply frustrated with the incumbent.)

But other Republicans say they are as much or more concerned about Heikes, who is best known for his strong opposition to abortion rights.

One Republican strategist called the situation “really challenging for Dan.”

“There’s just nothing that can be done about the high rate of ballot exhaustion,” said the strategist, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly.

Peltola has benefitted from the ranked-choice system before, the strategist added, noting her 2022 special House election victory against two Republican opponents.

Sullivan campaign officials and their allies dispute that they can’t affect the rate at which Republican voters exhaust their ballots and have launched an education effort through mail, phone banks, text messages and door-to-door canvassing that one senior Sullivan official characterized as a $10 million investment. Their efforts are now likely to intensify with the election weeks away.

Ad Wars

Peltola and Sullivan have both complained about campaign ads that were relentless and, in their telling, untrue.

Strategists for both parties say they’ve rarely seen anything like what’s happened in Alaska this election cycle. Both parties are on track to spend more than $115 million combined by November on ads alone, according to AdImpact — even though the number of voters able to be swayed by advertising in a small state like Alaska might be as few as 30,000 (an estimate provided by multiple strategists).

Republicans, unsurprisingly, are launching a wave of attacks on Peltola focused on her alleged ties to “lower 48” Democratic leaders and the suspicion that she holds progressive political views.

Among the attacks, however, are direct references to a report from The New York Times last month that alleged Peltola mistreated people who worked for her. The story sparked outrage among Democrats in Washington, who said it was proof not that Peltola was unfit for public service but that her staffers needed to toughen up and recognize the stakes of the election they were working on.

Republicans continue to run with the allegations. At least one Sullivan-aligned super PAC, Last Frontier PAC, was using the allegation in an attack ad last week.

And the senator himself has referenced the report on the stump, saying at an event last week that it proved the Democratic candidate was “unfit to serve.”

Peltola has tried to keep the focus more on the economy. The state had been bashed economically because of the president’s policies, the former congresswoman said during a town hall at a senior center here last week, while many of the state’s residents were in jeopardy of losing health care coverage because of a Republican law backed by Sullivan.

“I feel like Alaskans have had it up to here,” she said. “I feel like Americans have had it up to here, and there is an appetite to correct what has been done even in the last few years.”

entries.title: Every Second Counts in the NFL. Somebody Tell the Commanders.
entries.summary: In the final seconds of a crucial game, Dan Quinn’s team couldn’t walk and chew gum at the same time.
entries.content:
As soon as the Washington Commanders assassinated their 85% chance to beat the New York Giants in overtime on Sunday at Northwest Stadium, I texted one of my longtime sports editors: “Good thing I’m not in the ‘fire the coach’ stage of my life, ‘cause I’d sure as hell fire Dan Quinn. What a ******.”

Now, after thinking, and having nightmares, about the worst brain-dead snafu I can recall in 70 years of watching Washington’s NFL team — plus listening to outraged experts on six different shows — I have one thought to add.

It’s possible that the Commanders did everything correctly, except for the last split second of their final play. One split second.

If Jayden Daniels had simply flipped the ball out of bounds — over the head of tight end Ben Sinnott, who was near the left sideline — instead of inexplicably holding it and getting tackled in the field of play, then the correct grade for the Commanders’ clock management in the final 55 seconds would be: A+.

Washington did everything perfectly in those final seconds, except the very last and most important thing: throw an incomplete pass (or spike the ball) to allow for a 42-yard field goal attempt, which the internet says NFL kickers make about 85% of the time.

It is absolutely incorrect, as some have said or implied, that the Commanders, once they reached the Giants’ 24-yard line, should have just spiked it and kicked it.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

That would ignore the 15% chance — far from insignificant — that rookie Drew Stevens would miss the kick. He’d already missed wide right on a PAT Sunday. The Giants kicker missed three field goals. It was a rainy afternoon and a wet field.

If Stevens had missed, the game would simply have continued, and the Giants would have had the ball at their 32-yard line, only about 30 yards from (long) field goal range.

Recent NFL miracles and debacles — like the Philadelphia Eagles losing in England on Sunday despite kicking off with a 2-point lead and just eight seconds to play — prove that every second matters.

Before the disaster, Washington did a perfect job of clock burning, moving to the line deliberately, barking several signals and sending a man in motion — any of which might have provoked an offside penalty against New York — before finally snapping the ball to Daniels just before the play clock expired and with 13 seconds on the game clock.

A quick drop back and throw away, plus the time needed for the field goal attempt, would have left the Giants with only about eight seconds if they got the ball after a missed kick.

This interpretation, one of many ways to view this epic football blunder, may give the Commanders too much benefit of too many doubts. I think it’s the most likely reality, but one that the team’s coaches shy from explaining clearly because it dumps more blame on Daniels, and less on themselves, after a game in which JD5 played bravely and very well.

What many have missed, and I’ve been looking for in every game analysis, is that at the 55-second mark, the Commanders had not one but two absolute imperatives: Make sure you get off a field goal attempt, and run off as much time as you (safely) can before that kick in case you miss.

Turns out that, even in this most generous of evaluations, the Commanders couldn’t walk and chew gum at the same time. And historians recall that Quinn is also the coach, then in Atlanta, who blew the biggest lead in Super Bowl history to New England, in part because of widely criticized clock management.

During those 55 seconds, the Commanders certainly looked confused. After Daniels was tackled, for a second — a long time in the NFL — he did not even bounce up and rush to get the ball snapped and spiked. So, any variety of miscommunication is possible between Quinn, rookie offensive coordinator David Blough and Daniels during that time. But Quinn, Blough or both needed to be in the quarterback's earpiece with, “Above all, we have no timeouts left so Stop The Damn Clock!”

Also, Washington may have put too much emphasis on trying to gain a few more yards with (presumably) a short sideline pass that would either be caught or go out of bounds. Quinn said something along those lines afterward, implying he should have “made things easier” for Daniels by just “telling him to spike it.”

The only absolutely correct play, since neither team had a timeout left, was to bleed the clock, as the Commanders did, then spike the ball with about 12 seconds left on the game clock.

Is the whole mess worth firing a coach who, by many accounts, is an exemplary fellow?

I wouldn’t. Not now. Not with the team, apparently, still behind him. Not after his classy accept-the-blame press conference, which allowed Daniels to also accept blame but not actually get as much flack as he might have.

With offensive and defensive coordinators, and countless assistant coaches, the truth is that an NFL head coach doesn’t have to do much lifting, heavy or otherwise, during a game.

Do you throw the challenge flag? Do you go for it on fourth down? Do you manage your time outs correctly? Do you manage the clock precisely — and certainly never botch it entirely — at the end of the half and the game?

There’s other stuff. When to stomp on your headset. When to turn your hat around (never).

But the real test: Who is the coach next year? Sunday contained a painful amount of information on that.

entries.title: The Commanders' Defense Collapsed in the Second Half — Again
entries.summary: After starting strong against the Giants, Washington surrendered touchdowns on three straight possessions.
entries.content:
The reaction to the final seconds of Sunday’s Commanders-Giants game has felt like the Watergate hearings: What did the players know about the timeout situation, and when did they know it?

But Washington’s blunder was preceded by a fourth-quarter collapse where they were outscored 14-0 by the Giants in the final 11 minutes of the game.

The Commanders offense didn’t help matters by punting on three of its final four possessions — the botched final play ending the other drive.

But once again, Washington had a strong showing in the first half before coming apart at the seams in the second.

After watching the All-22 film, it appears two things happened: The pass rush that gave Giants quarterback Jameis Winston fits all first half (and produced a strip-sack fumble) was nonexistent in the final two quarters, and the Commanders became more concerned with defending big plays than trying to stop New York’s offense.

Coming into Sunday’s game it was clear that the defense’s best chance for success was getting to Winston, who has been one of the least efficient quarterbacks in the league when under pressure.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

On this play in the third quarter, the defense sat back in what looked like a Cover 4 zone, ceding the underneath area to Giants receivers. Winston had Malik Nabers on a quick slant, but the Commanders initially sent six rushers.

Linebacker Sonny Styles dropped back into coverage at the last second, but the confusion allowed fellow linebacker K’Lavon Chaisson a free lane on the other side of the line to Winston, who had to throw the ball into the dirt rather than hit Nabers for what would have likely been a first down.

Giants All-22 1 (1376x767, AR: 1.79)
Washington was able to mix that pressure with its run defense, which was typically unrelenting in the first half. Defensive linemen penetrated the backfield while linebackers hit the gaps to meet ball carriers.

Case in point: Early in the third quarter, with the Giants facing a third-and-2, linebacker Frankie Luvu didn’t bite on backup quarterback J.J. McCarthy faking a handoff on a run-pass option. The stop cut New York’s drive short and forced a field goal attempt.

Giants All-22 2 (1376x761, AR: 1.81)
But that success did not last.

Winston was pressured on 20 of his 59 dropbacks Sunday. Eleven of those dropbacks occurred in the first three quarters. He was sacked twice, including the strip-sack fumble caused by Chaisson.

But starting with the Giants’ first possession of the fourth quarter, Washington rarely put the heat on Winston. He was pressured on just nine dropbacks across the fourth quarter and overtime, completing five of nine passes for 45 yards and a touchdown.

On a second-and-5 at about the 10-minute mark, Winston was able to complete his three-step drop in a clean pocket and complete a 21-yard pass to tight end Theo Johnson.

Giants All-22 3 (1371x768, AR: 1.79)
A few plays later, the Commanders provided a lot of cushion on a fourth-and-8 from Washington’s 17-yard line. They seemed focused on not letting anything in the end zone and again ceded too much underneath.

Giants All-22 4 (2048x1144, AR: 1.79)
At the snap, the Commanders sent six rushers while the four defensive backs sat back in Cover 0, meaning man-to-man coverage and no over-the-top help. If you notice, that's only 10 players accounted for. The 11th was 320-pound defensive tackle Daron Payne, who also dropped back to cover any shallow crossing routes.

But tight end Isaiah Likely ran a quick slant that placed him between Payne and the closest defensive back. He hauled in a 16-yard touchdown that pulled New York within seven points.

Giants All-22 5 (1366x768, AR: 1.78)
On New York’s final possession of regulation, they made it to Washington’s 17-yard line. The Commanders again dialed up Cover 0 and provided 10-yard cushions to Giants receivers. Corner Mike Sainristil, who was benched after Week 2 due to consistent breakdowns in coverage, had Nabers as his assignment.

The Washington pass rush was unable to get pressure on Winston due in part to running back Cam Skattebo providing pass protection against a blitzing Jeremy Reaves.

Sainristil bit on Nabers’ jab step to the outside, opening up the middle of the field for the 17-yard touchdown grab that would send the game to overtime.

Giants All-22 6 (1180x648, AR: 1.82)
Coach Dan Quinn said Monday that the defense mixed in more man coverage to balance out the zone looks, but he was upset about the execution, no matter what scheme they were in.

“The end-of-the-game play is the one that's the glaring one from the game,” Quinn said. “But there's a number of spots in the fourth quarter that we thought, offensively, defensively, [special] teams — these are our chances to close the door.”

As the Commanders head to San Francisco next week to take on the 5-0 49ers, they could face the same issues that New York presented in the second half on Sunday. Quarterback Brock Purdy is the third-least-pressured quarterback in the NFL, according to NFL Research, having been sacked just three times through five weeks. When blitzed — something Washington does at the second-highest rate in the league — Purdy has the second-highest quarterback rating (136.5) behind only Baltimore’s Lamar Jackson (139.0).

entries.title: Homes With a Wood-Burning Fireplace — For Under $1 Million — in D.C., Maryland and Virginia
entries.summary: Our weekly column compares home listings across the DMV.
entries.content:
Wood-burning fireplaces sometimes generate heated conversations. For those who love them, moving to a home with a gas fireplace — or no fireplace at all — is unthinkable. The idea of spending a winter without the sound of crackling logs and the scent of woodsmoke would just be chilling.

On the other hand, there are plenty of people who prefer the simplicity of a gas fireplace, particularly if you can take the easy route of lifting a remote control to warm up a room or click it off. This side of the fireplace argument will lean on the mess of managing firewood and ashes.

If you are a bit romantic, though, an old-fashioned wood-burning fireplace is likely to warm your heart. We found options in D.C., Maryland and Virginia for homes priced under $1 million to meet that desire, including a townhouse, a condo and a single-family home.

Which one would you choose? Or, have a comparison you’d like to see in an upcoming column? Let us know at metro@washingtonsun.com.

entries.title: It’s 2026. Do You Know Who Your Landlord Is?
entries.summary: It’s not easy to find out who owns D.C. housing, and advocates say that’s complicating code enforcement.
entries.content:
Whether you’re a curious tenant, a city employee trying to issue a fine or an attorney looking to sue, there are many reasons you might want to know who owns a rental property in D.C.

In searching for an answer, good luck tracking down an actual human.

The city’s Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection collects information (on a newly revamped website) about who has a stake in the LLCs, nonprofits, co-ops and for-profit corporations that own housing in D.C. New York City may be the only other jurisdiction in the country that does so, Rebecca Janovich, DLCP’s superintendent of corporations, told The Washington Sun.

But because of how the law defines a “person,” sometimes that search just churns up another business entity. Advocates say that difficulty in determining who actually owns housing, and how much, is partly why it’s been so challenging to hold bad actors accountable, and why D.C.’s Department of Buildings is owed almost $87 million for unresolved code violations.

“I saw an example the other day: limited partnership, the beneficial owner listed as LLC. You go to the LLC, the beneficial owner is listed as an LLC. You go to that LLC, and finally you find an individual,” testified Beth Mellen, an assistant deputy attorney general for D.C., at an October housing committee hearing. “We support changes that would require those disclosures to get down to the natural person, so you don't have to follow the chain.”

The DOB has signaled that it wants to more proactively perform housing inspections by grouping different aliases used by property owners, Keith Parsons, the department’s director of strategic enforcement, told The Sun. But advocates want to go further, and have DLCP require that a “natural person” be listed, with contact information, alongside each LLC in a public-facing registry.

“We need to have a sense of landlords' full property portfolios, and so that once we know, ‘Oh, this landlord has bad practices,’ we want to be able to know all of the buildings in D.C. that they own, and then target our housing code enforcement accordingly,” Makenna Osborn, a senior attorney with the Children’s Law Center, told The Sun.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

With a centralized registry, advocates hope that D.C. agencies can better perform “clean hands” certifications, ensuring that landlords receiving city business don’t owe fines and penalties under a different LLC. Currently, the DLCP issues these certifications by checking a separate database managed by the Office of Tax and Revenue.

“Our systems are not talking to each other,” Ward 5 council member Zachary Parker told The Sun. “There is a lack of clarity around the ‘clean hands’ process and whether or not there is a vetting of beneficial owners and any potential connection to properties with outstanding fines. … We have a system that essentially allows many landlords to go without enforcement or consequences.”

Though there’s no legislative proposal pushing for a comprehensive, public-facing registry yet, Parker said he’d most likely support creating one. He batted away the privacy concerns DLCP had raised at a previous housing committee hearing.

“There is a difference between legal protections, which is why one creates LLCs, and the public's right to know who is doing business with the District and/or owning property,” he said. “There's public information shared for a wide range of things, including court cases, right? We're able to figure it out with the courts. I'm sure we can figure it out at DLCP.”

Not everyone is convinced that another registry is a vehicle for fixing poor housing conditions in the District. At another recent housing committee hearing, dozens of landlords said tenants’ sustained nonpayment of rent and a slow-marching eviction process is preventing them from injecting capital back into their properties.

“Another public registry is the tenant advocacy bureaucracy outdoing itself with another unnecessary burden, and it couldn't come at the worst time,” said Dean Hunter, the CEO of D.C.’s Small Multifamily & Rental Owners Association. “We have a rent payment crisis that has deeply destabilized affordable housing. I believe we're about six months away from a wave of affordable housing foreclosures.”

Advocates say it’s more of an enforcement issue than a burden. Since 2012, there’s been a D.C. law on the books requiring agencies to “maintain and access up-to-date records of outstanding fines, fees, penalties, interest, taxes, or other charges that may be owed by applicants for licenses or permits from the District government.”

That’s never happened, and until it does, “it will continue to be difficult to strategically and holistically hold the worst actors accountable,” Osborn said.

“There are a lot of people focused on this issue right now,” she said. “So hopefully there is momentum for really having a cross-agency, collaborative effort to have this be something that the government is focusing on.”

entries.title: Trump Administration Refills the Reflecting Pool After Months of Setbacks
entries.summary: The president said that he plans to visit the site once renovations are complete.
entries.content:
Trump administration officials refilled the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool over the weekend, the latest development in a monthslong saga affecting the monument.

On Saturday, a National Park Service sign posted on the pool’s wraparound fencing read: “The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is being refilled as the National Park Service and contractors put the final touches on a historic effort to clean, repair and beautify this national landmark.

“As part of the normal refilling process, the water may temporarily appear cloudy before clearing. The Reflecting Pool will once again stand as a fitting reflection of the beauty, dignity and grandeur of the Lincoln Memorial and our nation’s capital.”

Last week, President Donald Trump said the attraction would soon be restored to its former glory.

“I think they’re going to fill it up this week,” the president told reporters on Oct. 6. “The Reflecting Pool is totally complete, and we changed the old pipes.”

Trump added that he’ll visit the site once renovations are complete.

The storied landmark had undergone a botched renovation earlier this year, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia said in court filings.

The Trump administration spent roughly $16 million on repairs and renovations to the Reflecting Pool, government contract records show, but those efforts resulted in a massive algae bloom and a peeling lining.

The developments represented a setback for the president, who made renovating the monument a central fixture of his plan to “beautify” Washington. Following the botched renovation, Trump repeatedly asserted that the site had been the target of vandalism — and that saboteurs, not shoddy contracting work, were responsible for the situation.

Trump first announced a plan to refurbish the pool in April, saying that the attraction had been the subject of numerous complaints over its cleanliness. There were also issues with its leaky foundation, which the National Park Service said caused the pool to leak 16 million gallons of water a year.

The president announced the pool’s basin would be painted “American flag blue” ahead of the country’s 250th anniversary celebrations.

But the renovations led to peeling paint and algae blooms. On the Fourth of July, the landmark was fenced off to visitors.

Marcus, a German visitor who requested that only his first name be used, was not impressed by the sight.

“Everything I see is fenced,” the senior executive defense adviser told The Washington Sun on Saturday. “This is fenced; the White House is fenced.”

He questioned whether the Trump administration’s decision was worth it.

“What’s wrong here?” he said. “It’s supposed to be a democracy where everybody can walk around.”

The Washington Sun has emailed the National Park Service for information on when the pool will be reopened to visitors.
