entries.title: Supreme Court Sides With Trump Administration in DOGE Records Lawsuit
entries.summary: The White House has argued that DOGE is exempt from FOIA’s requirements as a presidential advisory body.
entries.content:
By Michael Kunzelman

The Supreme Court, siding with the Trump administration, agreed on Tuesday to hear arguments in a watchdog’s lawsuit seeking public records about trillionaire Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency.

The high court is intervening for a second time in Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington’s case, which seeks access to DOGE records from its operations in the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term.

Last year, the high court reined in a district court’s order for the government to produce DOGE-related records to CREW. The high court’s conservative majority concluded in June 2025 that U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled too broadly in ordering documents to be turned over to the group.

CREW claims DOGE is a federal agency and therefore is subject to the Freedom of Information Act.

The Trump administration argues that DOGE is exempt from FOIA’s requirements as a presidential advisory body.

Cooper ruled in CREW’s favor and ordered expedited processing of the group’s records request. An appeals court panel also sided with CREW.

The administration claims the panel ignored the Supreme Court’s direction to consider separation-of-powers concerns and intruded on the “autonomy and confidentiality” of presidential advisers.

“Subjecting advisory bodies to intrusive discovery triggers the very concerns that Congress sought to avoid by excluding presidential advisory bodies from FOIA’s reach,” Justice Department attorneys wrote.

The administration also says the appeals court impermissibly authorized the plaintiffs to take a sworn deposition of DOGE acting administrator Amy Gleason.

CREW says the appeals court fully complied with the Supreme Court’s previous order. The group also asserts that the public has a right to know how DOGE helped the administration carry out a sweeping overhaul of government operations in 2025.

“Undisputed facts in the public record — including the President’s statements — confirmed that (DOGE) was wielding enormous independent authority across the federal government,” its attorneys wrote.

entries.title: White House Says It Asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to Resign as Greece Ambassador
entries.summary: Guilfoyle has been under fire following media reports she pressured a donor to pay off her debt before her confirmation.
entries.content:
The White House has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign as U.S. ambassador to Greece, press secretary Katie Zacharia said Tuesday.

According to reporting by The Wall Street Journal last week, Guilfoyle asked Trump donor Eric Deters to cover a $100,000 credit card bill shortly before her confirmation hearing and offered him access to administration officials in return. Guilfoyle also reportedly told guests at a reception that the United States would destabilize the Greek government if it wanted to. The ambassador’s lawyer has said she did nothing wrong.

“She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well,” Zacharia said.

President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio had been weighing her dismissal, The Associated Press reported over the weekend. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-New Hampshire), Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California) and other Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation and her removal.

This is a developing story that will update.

entries.title: What We’ve Learned About the Caps Through Their First Five Games
entries.summary: At its best, this revamped group has looked like a legitimate playoff contender.
entries.content:
It’s been more than a week since the new-look Capitals (3-2) opened the season with a resounding win over Hurricanes. The four games since have been … somewhat choppier. Here’s what this group has shown so far.

This group has a far higher ceiling than last season …

These opening games have offered quite a bit for Caps fans to enjoy. The Alex Tuch–Pierre-Luc Dubois–Tom Wilson line has been a 200-foot marvel. Boone Jenner has made for a delightfully competent veteran presence on the fourth line. Vincent Desharnais has packed a punch on D. With these acquisitions, Washington added meaningful size, depth and speed, and that’s been clear from the jump.

“We all want to find our role right away, and I think we’ve done that,” said Jenner, who came to Washington in free agency this summer after playing 13 seasons in Columbus. “This room, the character that we have, I think everybody’s pulling the same way, and it makes it easy coming in.”

There have certainly been some real areas of frustration (read on for those), but at its best, this group has played like a legitimate contender, even if that has come only in fits and starts.

… but they still have plenty to clean up.

This much was obvious for anyone who caught a few minutes of Sunday’s third period against the Kraken. The loss ended up being a display of this group at its most uncoordinated — clumsy and inefficient, frequently giving away the puck, consistently playing from behind. “We’re just making too many mistakes,” Capitals coach Spencer Carbery said afterward. “A lot of mistakes with the puck. Poor decisions. We’ve just got to work on being a smarter team.” This was just one game. (Albeit one that proved exceptionally rough to watch.) But it did hint at some larger frustrations here.

The Capitals have been scoring above league average to begin the season. (Their shooting percentage is above the NHL average, too.) But they’ve done that despite struggling to get the puck in the offensive zone and keep it there: Washington ranks 30th in time spent in the o-zone.

“We’ll get it fixed,” Carbery said. “But it’s going to take some time, and guys have to learn.”

This defense needs Matt Roy (or Rasmus Sandin).

Washington has spent much of the season without its top defenseman: Matt Roy played the first two games of the season but has been sidelined since with a lower body injury — the Capitals placed him on injured reserve on Monday. That has proven to be a problem.

The defense has been shaky and uneven without him. Dylan McIlrath has not exactly inspired confidence as his replacement. (The penalty-prone veteran got scarcely five minutes of ice time in the loss against the Kraken on Sunday.) By moving Roy to the IR on Monday, the organization was able to recall a replacement from Hershey in Justin Holl, who could see the ice this week. But it’s hard to cover the absence of Roy, who remains day-to-day, though he’s been skating in a non-contact jersey.

Another defenseman this group is missing? Rasmus Sandin. He’s continuing to make his way back from the torn ACL he suffered in April. (Though it’s worth noting that he’s been skating for weeks and is said to be progressing well: “It’s very positive, how he looks right now,” Capitals general manager Chris Patrick said during training camp.) For all the Capitals’ depth at forward, they have precious little on their defense, and that’s been frustratingly clear this season.

Alex Tuch has made himself right at home. 

None of the Capitals’ additions has looked quite so comfortable as quickly as Alex Tuch. “He's an extremely intelligent player, and he has a great stick,” Carbery said. “Because of his instincts, he can read what's about to happen.” He’s been an early scoring threat, leading the Capitals in goals with three, and has been a key contributor to both the power play and the penalty kill. He’s shown a knack for controlling play and positioning himself well. No forward on the roster has produced more expected goals.

“He puts himself in the right spots to create offense,” said linemate Tom Wilson.

Tuch was among the splashiest acquisitions of the offseason, coming to Washington from Buffalo in a sign-and-trade with an eight-year, $84 million deal back in June. So far, he’s backed it up.

The power play is a work in progress.

Certainly, there have been flashes of a cleaner, more fluid power play. But that hasn’t yielded much in the way of consistent results: The Capitals have started the season 2-for-17 on the man advantage. So far, they haven’t gotten anything from their most reliable threat here, Alex Ovechkin, who leads the roster in power play minutes as usual, even as his ice time has decreased at even strength.

These units are the responsibility of a new coach: Washington added power play specialist Ray Bennett to the staff this offseason.

“I’ve liked what Ray’s doing, and what he’s trying to implement,” Carbery said after Washington scored its first power play goal of the season last week. “Now, this is at the base level of building this thing, so we’re not getting ahead of ourselves. But we have seen baby steps.”

Like any baby steps, however, those have come with some face-plants.

entries.title: Emmer Gathers Republican Newbies at Border in a Texas Party Poised to Make Gains
entries.summary: “This is the beginning of the relationship that these guys are going to have with their own people,” Emmer said.
entries.content:
McALLEN, Texas — Despite the headwinds across the country, House Republicans feel bullish about their chances to expand their grip in what’s been a solidly red state, thanks to midcycle redistricting.

Roughly a month before the midterms, House Majority Whip Tom Emmer traveled to the southwest border and gathered nine of the GOP’s top recruits competing in districts across the state for fundraisers and meetings, as the party faces the prospect of losing its majority.

Texas was where Republicans launched the redistricting war that spread across the country, and leaders still believe they’re poised to pick up at least three seats in the state. But the shuffling of the map also produced over a dozen new candidates who have very little, if any, relationship with House Republican leadership.

The Minnesota congressman used the trip as a way to not only build relationships with a bloc of candidates who are poised to join the conference next year but to also get them to bond with each other.

“This is the beginning of the relationship that these guys are going to have with their own people,” Emmer told The Washington Sun.

Mark Teixeira, a World Series champion with the New York Yankees now favored to win a seat in the Austin area, co-hosted the trip with the GOP whip. Joining them were Chris Gober, a longtime attorney and political operative who led the redistricting effort in Texas and is running for a seat representing the suburbs of Houston and Austin, and Republican candidates Steve Toth, Jace Yarbrough, Brandon Herrera, Carlos De La Cruz, Alex Mealer, Tano Tijerina and Jon Bonck.

In addition to touring the southern border, the group also held a roundtable with local business officials, a meeting with the border patrol council and a session with local ranchers.

While most of these candidates are competing in solidly red districts, Emmer acknowledged the broader economic environment is still a challenge for his party. Gas prices have soared to more than $4 a gallon, and grocery prices continue to increase because of the war in Iran and other Trump administration policies, putting GOP candidates on the defensive.

“Look, $4 gas, $6 diesel is unacceptable. I think we all agree on that,” Emmer told The Washington Sun. “But it's still not enough to vote for a communist.”

Republican leaders’ messaging has homed in on painting a stark difference between the ideologies of the Republican candidates and their Democratic opponents.

Emmer argued that some of the Republicans in Texas are doing better than polls suggest, saying he can see the dynamics on the ground when he’s in their districts.

“With De La Cruz and Herrera, if you are evaluating them from Washington, you may have a different opinion,” Emmer said. “‘You know, this is just typical rhetoric: ‘It's in the polling,’ It's all I have, right? So, I gotta go based on what it's saying, [but] you get here, you see them. These are top-notch candidates, which, that's the first thing you need. And they're doing the right things in their races.”

Emmer’s presence here has a dual purpose: He’s touching gloves with some potential new members of the conference who will not only be his colleagues, but also vote in leadership elections shortly after the midterms. Regardless of the outcome of the election, Emmer is expected to run for whip again.

Outside discussing immigration and farm policy, developing bonds is something that this group of Texas Republicans are already taking very seriously. The Texas delegation in the House has long been a force and significant voting bloc.

During the midterm convention last month in Dallas, Gober hosted an event for fellow Texas candidates. The goal was for everyone to meet and get to know one another in a more relaxed setting, he said.

“There's limited time to build those relationships with people,” Gober told The Sun. “So one thing I kind of understood, now was this unique opportunity to start building that, because once we get to orientation, once we're all kind of running around trying to figure things out, you lose kind of that ability.”

Alex Mealer, the Republican nominee in a newly drawn seat in the Houston area, is one of the candidates who has used these opportunities to get to know her colleagues. Mealer said that Emmer has, so far, been the only member of Republican leadership to come to her district. Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, who has aspirations for a leadership post and could challenge House Majority Leader Steve Scalise next Congress, also traveled to campaign with her, she said.

“Emmer very early on was one of the first mentors from the Congress,” Mealer told The Sun. “We will win my race, but I haven't had the opportunities as the others to travel around as much, just because we've been making sure we get across the finish line. With this many races, I appreciate him making time.”

entries.title: Judge Orders the Trump Administration to Halt Work on East Potomac Until Oct. 26
entries.summary: U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes put a further pause on tree-cutting at the historic D.C. golf course.
entries.content:
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes on Tuesday ordered a halt to tree-cutting at the East Potomac Golf Course until October 26, putting a further pause on work at the historic D.C. course that has been part of President Donald Trump’s plans to remake the city.

Reyes issued the order one day after a tense three-hour hearing in which she harshly criticized the government for having deceived her with its actions over the holiday weekend.

At that hearing, Reyes ordered a 24-hour pause that could be extended to 14 days if necessary. It was limited to one day while the government tries to find a key Trump administration official to discuss why a massive tree-cutting at the park needed to occur over the holiday weekend, with little notification to plaintiffs in a lawsuit trying to halt renovation plans or the judge.

The judge also ordered during that period the government “must provide the court and plaintiffs three business days’ written advance notice prior to making any irreparable modification to any permanent form or feature of the East Potomac Golf Course.”
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Makes a Shaky First Impression
entries.summary: Her first press briefing lasted about 15 minutes and sparked questions from current and former officials about her fitness for the role: “She needs to get much better fast.”
entries.content:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia’s first press briefing lasted less than 15 minutes, and she took just a handful of questions. The shaky debut, in which she made news about the administration asking for embattled Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle’s resignation but appeared nervous while speaking with reporters, led some Republican strategists and at least one White House official to question her fitness for the role.

“Getting behind the podium is tough, but she got off on the wrong foot. She needs to get much better fast, otherwise she'll break Scaramucci's record,” a White House official told MS Now, referring to Anthony Scaramucci, whom President Donald Trump fired in 2017 after 11 days as communications director.

Trump defended Zacharia following the press briefing, saying that “she was very good.”

A GOP strategist who supports Zacharia told The Washington Sun in a text message, "That was interesting." Another Republican operative told The Sun that Zacharia’s performance was a hard watch.

Those strategists, along with other officials and former officials The Sun talked to, spoke on the condition of anonymity out of fear of retribution from the Trump administration.

Zacharia devoted much of the briefing to touting Trump’s accomplishments and upcoming campaign travel to Florida, Georgia and Kentucky. She took a few questions — including telling Fox News’ Peter Doocy that she would need to get back to him when asked if the U.S. is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine — but the new press secretary abruptly ended the event by saying Trump would take reporter questions soon as he left for Alaska.

"Well, I don't think she's going to last long," one reporter said in the briefing room, moments after Zacharia left.

A former Trump official defended Zacharia, saying that her nerves showed, but that she got through it by "dropping the hammer with news on Guilfoyle" and then pivoting to the president's departure.

Trump named Zacharia, a former adviser to Trump Media and conservative commentator on Fox News, to the role last week. She replaces Karoline Leavitt, who departed at the end of August.

“She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning,” Trump posted on Truth Social when announcing her new role. “She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA! I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary.”

Zacharia told the Washington Examiner that she plans to stay in the role until the end of Trump's second term, which would make her the longest-tenured chief spokesperson under Trump.

She had faced criticism already, as CNN reported that, in now-deleted tweets, she promoted debunked falsehoods and advocated for hardline immigration policies. She also criticized the Trump administration, saying the midterms "will be a bloodbath" if officials didn't start focusing on the right priorities.
entries.author: Andrea Padilla

entries.title: Republicans Issue Rare Rebuke to Trump Over Russian Oil Deal
entries.summary: Lifting sanctions “will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans,” said a letter signed by six Republican senators.
entries.content:
Six Republican senators joined their Democratic colleagues in a Tuesday letter opposing President Donald Trump’s deal with Russia over diesel exports, in a rare GOP stand against the administration.

Sens. Mitch McConnell (Kentucky), Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), Alan Armstrong (Oklahoma), Thom Tillis (North Carolina) and John Cornyn (Texas) signed the message rebuking Trump’s Oct. 9 agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to suspend American sanctions designed to block sales of Russian diesel.

Lifting the sanctions “will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans,” reads the letter, which was also signed by six Democrats, including Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, who is expected to chair the powerful Senate Foreign Relations Committee if his party takes over Congress' upper chamber next year.

“Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin’s murderous, illegal war. This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded,” the message continues.

Trump has said the deal will address the record-breaking spike in fuel prices, particularly diesel. The Trump administration’s war on Iran spurred retaliation that has disrupted the normal flow of oil and gas out of the Middle East.

But experts are doubtful that Russia’s promises to supply the U.S. with diesel in the coming months will significantly ease the price shock. And Washington has deflected calls to ease tensions with Iran and cast blame elsewhere — particularly on Ukraine, which has targeted Russian energy infrastructure in its effort to pressure Putin to respect Ukrainian sovereignty.

Congress passed legislation in September to tighten American sanctions on both Iran and Russia, which Trump signed into law. International law professors Michael Schmitt and Ryan Goodman said in a Tuesday article in a law and policy journal that the diesel deal “undermines” those sanctions and may represent the U.S. helping Russia in its “unlawful use of force.”

Trump maintains he is not abandoning Ukraine, which the U.S. has supported to varying degrees since Russian incursions into its territory in 2014 and 2022.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, the president said the U.S. has not stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv.

“We help them, but we’re really helping them get to a final answer. We want the war ended,” Trump said. “We’re working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end.”

The president has suggested Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is an obstacle to a Russia-Ukraine compromise and should be replaced, spurring backlash from European allies of the U.S. and Ukraine. Over the weekend, the Financial Times reported that U.S. officials had threatened to slow American weapons shipments for Kyiv unless Ukraine stops targeting Russian energy facilities.

entries.title: Hillary Clinton Launches ‘High Stakes’ Podcast Ahead of the Midterms
entries.summary: The former first lady and secretary of state is teaming up with technology journalist Kara Swisher for the limited series.
entries.content:
Hillary Clinton is launching a new podcast with tech journalist and podcast host Kara Swisher ahead of the midterms, part of an effort to promote Democratic candidates and push her priorities as the election nears its final stretch.

The show, titled “High Stakes,” will run weekly through Nov. 3, with the inaugural installment set to air on Wednesday.

Vox Media is producing and distributing the podcast. The company also hosts several of Swisher’s podcasts, including “Pivot” and “On With Kara Swisher.”

“What you pay for groceries, rent and health care is on the line,” Clinton said in a video promoting the launch of the limited series.

The cover art features Clinton and Swisher donning sunglasses and looking serious while checking their phones.

With a Republican trifecta controlling the White House and both chambers of Congress, Clinton believes the stakes of the midterm elections could not be any higher.

“If we don’t reverse this chaos and corruption and cruelty that is being visited upon us by this administration, we won’t recognize our country,” Clinton told The New York Times in an interview last week.

In 2016, Clinton was the Democratic nominee for president, but she ultimately lost to President Donald Trump. Clinton already had experience in the White House and executive branch, serving as the first lady during the presidency of her husband, Bill Clinton, in the 1990s — and then as the Secretary of State during President Barack Obama’s first term.

Clinton has remained relatively quiet this election cycle, but she issued her first endorsement last week of Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic Senate candidate running against Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter and commentator.

entries.title: University of Maryland Tennis Club Suspended for Racist Image
entries.summary: The image was reported by Howard University’s club tennis team.
entries.content:
The University of Maryland indefinitely suspended its club tennis team for distributing materials with racist imagery ahead of a tournament hosted by the school.

The image appeared in an information packet emailed to participants in a tournament hosted by the University of Maryland this weekend, the university said. The first page of the document included the Maryland state flag, with the coat of arms replaced by pointed white hoods associated with the Ku Klux Klan, according to Howard University's club tennis team, which first reported the graphic.

Upon learning of the materials on Saturday, the school suspended its tennis club, launched a student conduct investigation into team leaders and referred the matter to the University of Maryland Police Department for further investigation. The tournament continued, and UMD’s team forfeited its matches. The club’s student leaders sent an email to each participating school apologizing, according to the university.

“The University of Maryland is horrified and expresses its regret and sincere apology for the harm that this has caused,” university spokesperson Jordan Dunklee said in a statement to The Washington Sun.

The Howard club team is calling for the University of Maryland to publicly apologize to Howard University, launch a formal investigation into who created the image, provide sensitivity training for UMD’s tennis team leaders and make a donation to the National Museum of African American History and Culture.

“True accountability has yet to come,” the Howard team said in a statement posted on social media.

Wayne Frederick, Howard University’s interim president, thanked the University of Maryland in a statement Monday for its “commitment to accountability” by suspending the club tennis team and launching an investigation into its student leaders.

“As institutions of higher learning, we share a responsibility not only to confront acts of racism but also to foster communities where respect for the humanity of others is an expectation, not merely an aspiration,” he said. “Our shared humanity demands nothing less.”

The University of Maryland’s Black Student Union called the incident “deeply disturbing” in a statement posted to social media and thanked Vice President for Student Affairs Patty Perillo for reaching out to the organization directly following discovery of the image. Still, the group said administrative action is not enough to address the impact on Black students.

“Racism disguised as student programming is not an accident or victimless oversight; it is a direct assault on the dignity, safety, and belonging of our students,” the statement said. “While apologies and forfeited matches are a necessary starting point, true resolution requires confronting the culture that allows such behavior to occur in the first place.”

The University of Maryland club tennis team did not immediately respond to questions from The Sun.

entries.title: The Timing of Trump’s Big Iowa Steel Mill Announcement Is Raising Eyebrows
entries.summary: The White House said the project was a “done deal” roughly one month before the midterms. The company behind it hasn’t bought land in the state yet.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump announced the “largest steel plant in American history” would be built in Iowa, where Republicans are facing several competitive races. “This deal is done,” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said alongside the president in the Oval Office, roughly one month before the midterms.

The deal is far from done.

As of Tuesday, the company behind the project, Mesabi Metallics, and its Indian parent company, the Essar Group, did not own property in Lee County, Iowa — where the plant is supposed to be built — or in the state of Iowa, according to The Washington Sun’s review of property records. The Des Moines Register reported that residents were approached by the company in September about purchasing land.

Mesabi Metallics told The Sun that the company “has secured land in Iowa for the project,” but declined to disclose additional details about where it was in the process of buying land.

“We are grateful to the local landowners who have worked with us openly and fairly throughout the process,” a Mesabi Metallics spokesperson, who declined to be identified, said in a written statement.

The timing of the announcement has raised eyebrows among both Democratic and Republican state lawmakers, who were told months ago that Iowa was in competition with several other states, including Arkansas, for the steel mill. Some said they feared the midterms played an outsized role in the announcement, and the president was getting ahead of actual plans — possibly to the detriment of Iowans.

“Why here, as opposed to a state that has a history of working with steel? We have multiple competitive elections, both statewide and congressional and U.S. Senate, in this state this year,” Iowa state Sen. Janice Weiner, the state’s Democratic leader, said. “Arkansas does not, and Arkansas would be a more traditional place to have steel.”

Trump announced on Sept. 28 that Mesabi Metallics would invest $15 billion in the Iowa steel complex. The president told reporters that the mill would create 6,000 construction jobs and 1,750 permanent jobs. Several Iowa Republicans in tight races this November, including Rep. Ashley Hinson, who’s running for Senate, and incumbent Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, joined the president for the announcement.

When asked at the announcement whether the project was contingent on tax breaks in Iowa, Lutnick said that “the president doesn’t bring people together unless it’s a done deal.”

But after Trump’s announcement, Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, a Republican, called state legislators back to the capitol for a special session to consider major tax incentives for the company.

Weiner told The Sun that the deal did not meet her expectations for protecting Iowans. The tax break nearly doubled the amount that had been discussed earlier. And Democrats could not get the company to guarantee that the 6,000 construction jobs would go to Iowa workers or whether permanent workers would be able to collectively bargain for pay or benefits, she said. On Oct. 2, the Republican-led House and Senate passed the tax breaks, with two Republicans voting against it in the House and with six Republican holdouts in the Senate.

At the special session, Republican state Sen. Dan Dawson, who voted against the tax breaks, said the negotiations with the company were happening in the governor’s office rather than with the Iowa Economic Development Authority.

“Do I believe the Iowa taxpayer received the best deal in this proposition? Absolutely not,” Dawson said on the statehouse floor.

The governor’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

Mesabi Metallics’ financial history has also raised questions about the plan. The company declared bankruptcy in Minnesota in 2016 while trying to build an iron ore complex there. After years of financial turmoil, that ore complex opened last week, nearly two decades after the project was announced.

The political salience of a new steel mill, however, became immediately apparent after Trump’s announcement.

Miller-Meeks, whose district includes Lee County and is running in a tight race against Democratic former state Rep. Christina Bohannan, hailed the project in an interview with Fox News last month.

“The state of Iowa has been very forward in competing to get this business to come to Iowa. This is a part of our state that has high unemployment and it has the lowest wages, so this is extremely significant,” Miller-Meeks said.

Miller-Meeks has a history of winning tight races. In 2020, Miller-Meeks won by six votes, and in 2024, she beat Bohannan by fewer than 1,000 votes. Both of those races went to a recount.

In the Senate race, which has become increasingly competitive in recent months, both Hinson and her Democratic opponent, Josh Turek, have campaigned on the steel mill.

“I just think about the countless opportunities for Iowa families and what this means for them. It is a game changer for our state, and frankly, for the country,” Hinson said at the Oval Office press conference.

Turek, a current state representative, voted in favor of the tax incentives for the steel mill.

“I was proud to vote in favor of this. I mean, we are a state that is uniquely hurting. We're one of three states seeing our economy contract,” Turek said during a debate last Wednesday. “This plant could honestly be transformative.”

But while many Republicans have credited Trump’s tariff policies for the forthcoming steel mill, Turek said the president’s trade agenda has “hurt Iowa more than any other state.”

Other Democrats are campaigning on the issue, but they remain more skeptical about the tax breaks given to the company and protections for workers.

“This is a promising idea for Lee County and for our state given that our economy is among the worst in the nation,” said Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand in a statement on X. “I look forward to hearing more details, particularly on what protections for Iowa taxpayers will be built into the deal, and what guarantees will exist for Iowa workers to build and work in the plant if Iowa taxpayers will be asked to chip in.”

Trump’s manufacturing announcements have not always panned out. In his first term, Trump promised that a $10 billion manufacturing facility built by Foxconn Technology Group would open in Wisconsin, creating 13,000 jobs. The project was later scaled back to a $672 million facility that created fewer than 1,500 jobs.

“Oftentimes, with industrial policy, projects get cited not for their economic value but their political value, and that, of course, perversely makes it harder for the project actually to come to fruition,” said Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics and trade policy at the Cato Institute.

Trump’s track record has left some lawmakers and trade experts concerned about how long the project will take and how beneficial it will be to Iowa. The White House and Mesabi Metallics told The Sun that they expect the plant to start production in 2030.

“When you see Iowa spiraling pretty quickly from red to blue, and then you see this announcement made mere days before the election with a Republican legislature calling an emergency one-day session to funnel $1.4 billion dollars to this project, it just screams political desperation,” Lincicome added.

The White House defended Trump’s record in a statement to The Sun and reasserted plans for the Iowa steel complex.

“The President has a proven record of securing historic investments, creating high-paying jobs, and bringing manufacturing back to the United States,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said. “This is going to be the first mega-steel plant built in our country since the 1960s and is only possible because he rolled back burdensome red tape, reshored industry, and created an environment for companies to build in America again.”

entries.title: House Republicans Launch Investigation Into D.C. 'Jury Nullification’
entries.summary: Rep. James Comer’s office said it sent letters to two D.C. activist groups that have been training D.C. residents on jury duty.
entries.content:
The House committee overseeing local D.C. affairs has launched an investigation into “politicized jury nullification initiatives by left-wing activist groups,” Rep. James Comer (R-Kentucky) announced Tuesday.

The investigation is so far targeting two D.C. organizations, Harriet’s Wildest Dreams and Free DC, which have hosted a series of trainings called the Juror Information Project. Comer, who chairs the House Oversight Committee, alleges the groups are advocating for the long-debated practice of jury nullification, which happens when a juror opts to acquit someone — even if they think the accused person is technically guilty — because they object to the law or to the decision by prosecutors to charge the person.

Comer argues that the groups are undermining the rule of law.

“It is clear that the position of Free DC and Harriet’s Wildest Dreams is that potential jurors should not make decisions impartially based on applying the law as instructed to the facts presented before them in the case, but based on their subjective, personal beliefs and activist agendas,” he said in a news release Tuesday. “These shocking reports underscore the necessity of congressional oversight to protect against an assault targeting constitutional rights and processes.”

Comer’s office said it sent letters to two people associated with the groups. The Free DC co-founder named in Comer’s letter did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday. The Harriet’s Wildest Dreams co-founder named in Comer’s letter declined to comment.

Discourse around jury nullification in D.C. took on steam last year after a streak of cases where D.C. grand juries declined to indict people who had been arrested for allegedly assaulting federal officers. Grand juries almost always return indictments, and not doing so is exceedingly rare; the process is generally stacked in prosecutors’ favor. But the office of the Trump-appointed U.S. attorney for D.C., Jeanine Pirro, was asking grand juries for the indictments in the midst of a surge of federal law enforcement that has been deeply unpopular among D.C. residents.

Perhaps the most high-profile of those cases involved the so-called “sandwich guy,” who became a symbol of D.C.’s anti-Trump resistance after he hurled a sandwich at a federal agent in a self-described act of protest. Pirro’s office pursued him for felony assault, but a grand jury declined to indict on that charge. Then, prosecutors downgraded the charge to a misdemeanor, and another D.C. jury found the defendant not guilty after a trial. To find the “sandwich guy” guilty, the jury would have had to find that he generated a “reasonable apprehension of immediate bodily harm”; the defense argued that throwing a sandwich was harmless.

The string of incidents raised questions about whether jurors were declining to indict because they believed prosecutors had not presented enough evidence to establish probable cause, or because they disagreed with the decision to pursue charges in the first place. Without getting inside jurors’ heads, it’s impossible to know.

Jury nullification has long been a subject of debate among attorneys and legal scholars. Georgetown University law professor Paul Butler, in a Washington Post op-ed last year, called it “a powerful tool for slapping down politicized criminal justice” and said D.C. grand jurors were being patriotic when they rejected the charges Pirro’s office sought. The prominent libertarian group the Cato Institute has also supported the practice as a safeguard against government overreach. But critics of the practice argue that the legal system relies on jurors applying the facts to the law, not voting their conscience.

According to their public websites and social media posts, Harriet’s Wildest Dreams and Free DC’s workshops have discussed “what it really means to serve on a jury and how we can use that role to protect our people especially those with marginalized identities who are disproportionately targeted by the criminal legal system.”

“Jury duty is not just a civic responsibility; it’s a powerful tool for ensuring fairness and justice,” the groups wrote in a description of a September Juror Information Project session. “Come and engage in meaningful conversations, learn from legal experts, activists, and fellow community members, and find out how you can play a pivotal role in shaping a more just society.”

While the September event description did not explicitly mention jury nullification, the Washington Examiner reported in August that a leader at one of the sessions had spoken directly about the idea, saying: “You have this superpower, and that superpower is you are able to nullify that goddamn jury.” That quote made its way into Comer’s letters.

Comer’s office, in the letters, requested documents related to juror training and information about how the events have been financed, giving the groups a deadline of Oct. 27.

entries.title: Sotomayor, Gorsuch Criticize ‘Serious Constitutional Problems’ in Denied Immigration Case
entries.summary: The two justices from opposite sides of the high court’s ideological spectrum have teamed up once again to call out what they see as an “absurd” application of federal law.
entries.content:
Supreme Court Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Neil Gorsuch joined forces to issue a statement highlighting the “constitutional absurdity” of an immigration case that the high court declined to take up Tuesday.

Sotomayor, an Obama appointee, and Gorsuch, a Trump appointee, hail from opposite ends of the Supreme Court’s ideological spectrum. But the pair, which agreed 62% of the time during the most recent term, has teamed up in the past to express their concerns about cases and call for the consideration of specific issues in future litigation.

The justices did agree with the Supreme Court's decision to deny review for Jesus Herrera-Salazar’s case, a Mexican national convicted twice of being “found in” the U.S. without proper documentation. The pair concurred in part because Herrera-Salazar had already been removed from the country by the time his case reached the high court.

What Sotomayor and Gorsuch took specific issue with was lower courts’ disregard for the double jeopardy standard, which prevents an individual from being tried twice for the same crime.

Sotomayor and Gorsuch described the “serious constitutional problems that plague the Government’s treatment of Herrera-Salazar,” including a lower court’s 2020 indictment for Herrera-Salazar being “found” to be present in the U.S. after having received an order of removal and leaving the country years earlier.

After Herrera-Salazar pleaded guilty and served a 15-month prison sentence, authorities expressly instructed him not to leave the Eastern District of Oklahoma while serving on supervised release. He was later arrested and indicted under the same federal charge in 2022 — though he did not leave the country again and reenter unlawfully between his two convictions.

Herrera-Salazar appealed his case after the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals rejected his double jeopardy concerns by arguing that a separate reentry offense was not required to indict him in 2022.

By the appeals court’s logic, Sotomayor and Gorsuch asserted, Herrera-Salazar could have been charged with a separate violation “for each day that he was ‘found in’ prison while serving his sentence for the first conviction.”

“Absurd as that seems, it is a logical outgrowth of the Government’s contention” that Herrera-Salazar’s second conviction “poses no double jeopardy problem,” the justices wrote.

The justices also argued that the government had presented Herrera-Salazar with a Hobson’s choice — a seemingly free decision that only offers one real option — because “whether Herrera-Salazar remained in the Eastern District of Oklahoma or left the United States, he would be breaking the law.”

Sotomayor and Gorsuch encouraged the justice system to “give the Double Jeopardy Clause its full weight and meaning” if courts are tasked with reviewing cases similar to Herrera-Salazar’s.

President Donald Trump has pursued an aggressive stance on immigration policy and deportations since the start of his first term in 2017. The White House’s web page cataloging immigration policies and data reports that the Trump administration has deported more than 605,000 people, with additional 1.9 million individuals opting to self-deport rather than face immigration proceedings.

entries.title: How a Far-Right Conspiracy About Talarico’s Campaign Absence Fell Apart
entries.summary: Conservatives parroted a bogus rumor that Talarico was in an Ohio mental health facility during a nine-day absence from the campaign trail.
entries.content:
Far-right personalities spent the weekend amplifying a bogus online conspiracy theory that Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico received treatment at an Ohio mental health facility during a recent nine-day absence from the campaign trail — instead of being at home with the flu, as his team said he was.

The rumor fell apart following a comprehensive New York Times report published Monday that featured time-stamped security camera footage showing Talarico was at his Austin home between Oct. 1 and 8. However, that didn’t stop many of the provocateurs from continuing to parrot the claim.

Talarico resurfaced at the Austin City Limits music festival on Friday. The following day, he was photographed alongside country singer Kacey Musgraves at her Dallas concert.

After his appearances, some proponents of the conspiracy theory acknowledged it had been debunked — but insisted that did not matter because they were simply bringing attention to Talarico’s absence.

“It's not why you were missing. It's that you went missing,” Spencer Pratt, the former reality TV star-turned-failed Los Angeles mayoral candidate, wrote on X Monday. He was one of the theory’s biggest backers, behind Tesla CEO and X owner Elon Musk.

Questions about Talarico’s whereabouts began to circulate after his opponent in the Senate race, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, demanded “proof of life” last week.

The rumor itself appeared to originate from Pratt, who posted about Talarico’s absence Friday morning.

“My sources are telling me Talarico is in a mental health facility,” Pratt wrote. “His campaign has stopped actively planning events in the vital homestretch of the campaign.”

That claim was amplified by conservative commentators, including Musk.

Caroline Wren, a former Trump fundraiser, also wrote on X on Friday: “I can confirm that we have no credible evidence that James Talarico has not checked himself into a psych ward due to a complete mental breakdown.”

The next day, she added to the speculation with another post in which she insinuated a private plane carrying Talarico flew from Austin, Texas, to Ohio to transport the candidate to the Lindner Center, a private mental health facility and psychiatric hospital in Mason, where Harris County Judge Lina Hidalgo, another Texas Democrat, previously sought treatment.

On Sunday, Nick Sortor, a political content creator, released a recording of what he claimed was a hospital employee saying Talarico had been a patient at the facility.

But the center soon denied the claim.

“Representative James Talarico has never received treatment from Lindner Center of Hope,” the center wrote in a statement posted to X hours after the recording dropped.

A couple of hours later, Talarico reposted the statement along with his own: “I’ve never even been to Ohio.”

JT Ennis, Talarico’s spokesperson, called the rumor “a lie designed to promote a pathetic conspiracy theory.”

He reiterated: “Last week James Talarico was home in Austin, Texas, recovering from the flu.”

At least one conservative has apologized for amplifying incorrect information.

Political influencer Carmine Sabia wrote Tuesday on X: “I apologize for sharing the false report about James Talarico receiving mental health treatment. I relied on the reporting available then, but I got it wrong and retract it.”

“I support Ken Paxton, but the truth matters more than winning on a lie.”

entries.title: Press Groups Compare Gov. Moore’s ‘Censorship’ of Sinclair News Outlets to Trump's Media Ban
entries.summary: The accusations come amid the Maryland Democrat’s personal defamation suit against the broadcast group’s chair, David Smith.
entries.content:
Press-freedom groups urged Maryland Gov. Wes Moore to stop scuttling media inquiries from Sinclair-owned news outlets amid his defamation quarrel with the broadcast group’s chair, comparing the practice to President Donald Trump’s recent White House media ban.

In a Tuesday letter, officials from the Freedom of the Press Foundation and seven other press associations blasted Moore for referring routine inquiries from journalists at Sinclair affiliates into “legal review black holes.”

Last month, Moore condemned Trump for his decision to exclude CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from the White House press pool, accusing the president of having a “real problem” with free speech.

But in their letter, the press-freedom groups said Moore was essentially doing the same thing as the president.

“Personal litigation does not justify impeding reporting or reducing government transparency,” the letter says. “While government agencies under your watch stonewall reporters based on flimsy pretexts, you take to the airwaves to condemn the Trump administration’s unconstitutional ban of news outlets the president doesn’t like from the White House.”

The letter is the latest in a public feud between Moore and David Smith, the Sinclair chair, that culminated in Smith’s July defamation suit against the governor. Smith accused Moore of damaging his reputation after the governor told MS NOW that Smith had close ties to deceased child trafficker Jeffrey Epstein and that he bought The Baltimore Sun to "do Donald Trump's work.”

Now, state agencies have reportedly begun sending a generic response to all reporters at The Baltimore Sun, FOX45 News, 7News and Spotlight on Maryland — even when questions are entirely unrelated to Smith’s defamation suit.

“Because of the current lawsuit from Sinclair’s Executive Chairman, David D. Smith, against the Governor, we’re sending all media requests from Sinclair-affiliated outlets to our legal team for review. We’ll get back to you once that’s finished,” the Maryland email responses say, according to records published by The Baltimore Sun.

Moore’s office called the premise of the letter “completely false” and disputed that Maryland agencies are refusing to engage with Sinclair outlets.

“In the last week alone, state agencies and the Governor's Office have answered dozens of questions from Sinclair outlets,” the governor’s press secretary, Ammar Moussa, said in an email. “David Smith chose to sue the Governor. Having our legal team look over inquiries is basic due diligence, not a blackout.”

The friction began after the newspaper published an investigative series questioning Moore’s military record. Those articles drew mixed reception over their fairness and peculiar byline authors: The stories were penned by Drew Sullins, a Sinclair tech manager, and Sean Lawlor, Sinclair’s chief of security.

New York magazine reported that Sullins and Lawlor went beyond normal journalistic norms when they sent emails to Moore’s office saying that “it’s clear to anyone with even a modicum of common sense” that Moore “has a problem with telling lies that grossly exaggerate his record of accomplishment.”

Moore's team responded to the investigations with accusations that Smith had weaponized Sinclair outlets to damage the governor’s image and halt a potential 2028 presidential run.

“Marylanders deserve strong local journalism,” Moussa said at the time. “They do not deserve a newspaper being used as a political weapon by its owner.”

Moore acknowledged mistakenly claiming a Bronze Star on a 2006 White House fellowship application. He was ultimately awarded the medal in December 2024.

Seth Stern, the Freedom of the Press Foundation’s chief of advocacy, told The Washington Sun that Sinclair had not asked FPF to intervene, adding that, even if Moore’s concerns about Smith influencing coverage were entirely correct, “That is still not a basis for official retaliation.”

“It is not the job of state agencies to help the governor win a personal lawsuit,” he said.

The Washington Sun has a content-sharing agreement with The Baltimore Sun.

entries.title: Judge Halts USDA Relocation Plans, for Now
entries.summary: A judge found the department is “almost certainly” using funds in ways Congress didn’t contemplate when it appropriated them.
entries.content:
A federal judge on Tuesday halted the Agriculture Department’s plans to close offices and relocate employees across eight agencies, ruling that the department is likely violating spending restrictions Congress wrote into its appropriations laws.

In an order, U.S. District Judge Vince Chhabria of the Northern District of California stopped the USDA from closing offices or moving employees outside their local commuting area at the Forest Service, the Agricultural Research Service, the Food and Nutrition Administration and five other components while the litigation continues.

The order covers plans to move the Forest Service headquarters to Salt Lake City and close all nine regional offices, and to shutter all seven Food and Nutrition Administration regional offices, which could mean relocations for up to 870 of roughly 1,200 employees.

The restrictions at issue expire Dec. 11, so Congress could revisit them in its next funding bill, Chhabria wrote.

“If the agency wishes to move forward with its plans to close offices and relocate employees, it will soon have the opportunity to convince Congress of the merits of those plans,” Chhabria wrote. “Congress, if it agrees, can choose not to extend the restrictions at issue in this case.”

Chhabria found the USDA is “almost certainly” using funds in ways Congress didn’t contemplate when it appropriated them. He wrote that that counts as “reprogramming” under the law, and that Congress barred reprogramming for reorganizations without committee approval.

The judge said he had “no view” on whether the reorganization is a good idea, but he faulted the USDA for not analyzing the risks the reorganization could pose to the services the agency provides.

The lawsuit was brought by four federal-employee unions who represent eight USDA components named in the case. The suit grew out of a broader union challenge to President Donald Trump’s 2025 push to shrink the federal workforce, which is still pending before a different judge in the same court.

Elena Goldstein, a legal director at Democracy Forward, said the court’s “stay of USDA’s forced relocation plans will allow the vital work of the department and its employees to continue, protecting the families and communities across the nation that rely on its vital work.”

The USDA announced its reorganization in summer 2025, listing relocating employees outside the Washington area as one of four pillars. The unions argue the plan would force thousands of employees to choose between moving, often to another state, or losing their jobs.

Numerous employees told The Washington Sun in July that they would rather quit than move, which could create major disruptions for the agencies, citing the hundreds of employees who were lost after the USDA moved the Economic Research Service and National Institute of Food and Agriculture to Kansas City, Missouri, in 2019.

entries.title: ICE Wants to Use AI to Monitor Detainee Calls and Movements
entries.summary: The agency is looking for software to sort through a high volume of data, use voice recognition and maintain detainee caller profiles.
entries.content:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement is looking for an AI software that can monitor the phone and video calls and movements of immigrants at detention centers.

The system would use transcriptions and voice-recognition technology to monitor who detainees are talking to and the contents of the calls, as well as data from cameras, according to a document the agency posted Friday on a federal government contracting website.

ICE is looking for software that can integrate information it already gathers to generate leads on safety and security concerns and potential criminal activity that an employee would review. The document refers to the software as the “Suite” and it would run 24/7, storing profiles of detainees.

“ICE facilities generate authorized telephone, messaging, tablet, video-visitation, detainee management, movement, incident, and camera data at volumes that cannot be reviewed and correlated manually in a timely manner,” the document states.

The publishing of the request for information from potential contractors marks a preliminary step in finding a company to provide the service. Watchdog group Project Salt Box first reported on the document.

Immigration policy and data experts raised concerns about how ICE would use the data it could potentially gather to target undocumented families outside of detention. The proposed system is part of an expansion of AI that the Department of Homeland Security is using to track immigrants and citizens during the second Trump administration.

“It's basically bringing AI into the game of superpowering ICE even more,” said Todd Schulte, president of the immigrants’ rights advocacy group FWD.us.

While ICE already monitors detainees’ telephone and video calls that are not related to legal matters, the software would expand that surveillance through voice recognition. The aim would be to maintain profiles that track whether the person the detainee talks to in any given call is the person the software associates with the number dialed. ICE labeled the person not matching the associated phone number “receiver-side deception.”

Steven Hubbard, a senior data scientist at the American Immigration Council who has been keeping tabs on how the agency is using AI, said such a program could add to mistakes.

“Especially with biometric data, there can be lots of different errors that happen, and then once that is entered into the system, then it becomes sort of a black box where you don't know how AI is making those determinations or summarizations that can cause problems or create errors,” he said.

Using video camera feeds at the detention centers, the software would need to flag fights, falls, signs of aggression and self-harm, according to the ICE document. During President Donald Trump’s second term, people in ICE detention have committed suicide at an unparalleled rate, according to an Associated Press investigation.

Schulte and David Bier, the Cato Institute’s director of immigration studies, expressed skepticism that ICE would use the software to protect the detainees’ well-being.

“People are committing suicide because they feel hopeless and are cut off from their lives, and feeling like you can't communicate freely with people on the outside would potentially exacerbate that problem,” Bier said.

entries.title: Housing Groups Say Canceling HUD Funding Violated First Amendment Rights
entries.summary: The groups are trying a new line of attack against the Trump administration's decision to rescind $56 million in funding.
entries.content:
Housing groups say they have a new legal argument to challenge the Trump administration’s move to cancel more than $56 million in funding last month with a “pocket rescission” — and they got a judge to order the government to keep the funding from lapsing for now.

The lawsuit, filed by the National Urban League and groups from several states, argues that the administration’s decision to rescind the funding appropriated by Congress is unlawful under the First Amendment, because the White House cited housing groups’ engagement in “DEI-centric discriminatory agendas” as reasoning for the drastic cuts.

“What comes out of this will likely be new law,” said Lindsay Zimliki, one of the attorneys representing the housing groups.

The lawsuit, which came the day before federal funding for the Department of Housing and Urban Development’s Comprehensive Housing Counseling program was set to expire, is one of the latest attempts to challenge the pocket rescissions.

Under a previous separate challenge last year, the D.C. Circuit held that plaintiffs could not use the Administrative Procedure Act to challenge the rescission process. This time, the housing groups claim that the government discriminated against them and retaliated for their viewpoints.

“This is not a case about whether the federal government may subsidize speech that advances policies the Administration disfavors; it is a case of the Administration defunding and shutting down a program because it does not like the non-program-related viewpoints of the organizations that receive the funding,” the lawsuit says.

U.S. District Judge Jia M. Cobb ordered the administration to suspend the Sept. 30 funding lapse for the HUD program while the lawsuit moves forward.

The federal program funds nonprofits that help Americans with foreclosure prevention, mortgage counseling and buying and renting homes. The attempted cuts in this case are a fraction of $810 billion that the White House has sought to recoup from several agencies' programs across the country. Using a pocket rescission allowed the Office of Management and Budget to withhold funds until they expired at the end of the fiscal year.

The Government Accountability Office found that those rescissions amounted to a violation of spending law.

In court filings in the latest lawsuit, the Trump administration argued that the court “lacks statutory authority to suspend appropriations deadlines” and “control disputes” over the White House’s funding decisions.

And the administration asked Cobb to deny the plaintiffs’ First Amendment claim, stating that the housing group's free speech rights were not affected by the rescission.

As part of the reasoning to withhold funding for the housing groups, the administration also argued that the program was “wasteful” and had “nothing to do with the grantees’ viewpoint.”

“While Plaintiffs may have hoped for a subsidy from the Government to spread their message, they certainly were never entitled to one, and the Government does not violate the First Amendment by not providing one,” a Friday filing states.

Normally, when the White House proposes rescinding money that Congress appropriated, Congress has 45 days to vote on it. However, this rescission’s announcement came five days before the funds lapsed.

With the pocket rescission announcement coming so close to the end of the fiscal year, attorneys representing the housing groups said in an interview that notice of funding — which is how the different groups can apply for federal money — was “about six to seven months late,” and that grantees had covered services with the expectation of being reimbursed with funding that was never awarded.

entries.title: Trump Administration Cuts Refugees' Deadline to Contest Their Status Terminations
entries.summary: The policy does not say exactly how many people could be affected, but it specifically refers to refugees admitted during the Biden administration.
entries.content:
By Gisela Salomon

MIAMI (AP) — The Trump administration is cutting the time refugees have to contest the termination of their status, a move critics say could put tens of thousands of people who fled persecution and wars in their home countries on a path to deportation.

The new policy, which goes into effect Wednesday, reduces from 30 to 10 the number of days refugees have to challenge the revocation of their status. It is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to restrict and transform a program that has served for decades as a pathway for refugees.

The goal of the new policy, according to the document, is to “mitigate potential risks” associated with people who were admitted as refugees but were not eligible for refugee status.

The policy does not say exactly how many people could be affected, but it specifically refers to refugees admitted during President Joe Biden’s administration, when it says there was an “alarming erosion of the integrity” of the refugee program. Refugee advocates dispute that claim.

The Trump administration is already reviewing the cases of at least 185,000 refugees admitted during the Biden administration who still have pending green card applications.

Welcoming refugees has been a matter of bipartisan consensus in the United States since Congress passed the Refugee Act with overwhelming support in 1980. That law made refugee applications some of the most rigorously scrutinized within the immigration system.

Advocates and refugee resettlement groups condemn the new policy

Some maintain refugees will not have enough time to defend their status under the new policy.

“These families did everything asked of them,” said Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president of Global Refuge. “They submitted to interviews, background checks and years of waiting abroad, only setting foot on U.S. soil once government officials approved their applications.”

Now, she said, "the Homeland Security Department wants to revisit those decisions on a 10-day clock, a notice period wholly insufficient to find a lawyer, translate documents or get records out of a country they were forced to flee.”

HIAS, a major refugee aid group, warned that refugees who have fled violence, persecution and displacement will be at risk of being deported to the countries where they could face harm, persecution and torture.

“They are trying to upend the core principle that refugee resettlement represents permanent protection,” said HIAS vice president Naomi Steimberg.

Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The State Department referred questions to DHS.

The refugee program has been transformed

The Trump administration has drastically altered the refugee program and transformed it into a mechanism for resettling white South Africans in the country.

In September, the government announced plans to limit the total number of refugees admitted to the country in 2027 to 17,500, the majority of whom are white South Africans.

During his first administration, Trump slashed the number of refugees approved every year. The Biden administration built it back and set a goal of admitting 125,000 refugees during the final year of his term.

Upon returning to the White House for his second term, Trump immediately suspended the refugee program, stranding people around the world who had been slated to come to the U.S. Later the administration reopened the program and limited it mostly to white South Africans.

entries.title: Democrats Are Asking the FAA to Stop Using AI Air Traffic Control Tool
entries.summary: The tool, which has been rolling out in the D.C. region, won’t replace humans making the decisions, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.
entries.content:
A group of Democrats in Congress is asking the Federal Aviation Administration and the Transportation Department to stop using an AI tool to assist with D.C.-area flight management until they answer questions about its safe implementation.

The FAA and DOT launched the AI-enabled Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories (SMART) tool on Sept. 21.

The deployment in the D.C. region is part one of a phased rollout that began with a 90-day evaluation period before broader, nationwide use.

Twenty-five members of Congress addressed their concerns in an Oct. 9 letter to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford.

“We are deeply concerned about the integration of any AI-enabled system into air traffic control systems, where decisions are literally a matter of life or death,” said the letter signed by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (New York), LaMonica McIver (New Jersey), Rashida Tlaib (Michigan), Jamie Raskin (Maryland) and Sen. Chris Van Hollen (Maryland). D.C.’s nonvoting delegate, Eleanor Holmes Norton, also joined the letter.

The lawmakers wrote that they’re concerned about SMART assisting air traffic controllers and that Congress has not received safety evaluations, testing reports or information about how workers were trained to use the technology.

The letter referenced the Jan. 29, 2025, crash near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in which 67 people died after an American Airlines flight and an Army helicopter collided in midair.

SMART is currently being used to help with air traffic at DCA, Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall and Washington Dulles International Airport.

Last year, Congress appropriated $12.5 billion toward modernizing air traffic control systems in the wake of recent tragedies. The government built SMART through a 12-year, $875 million contract.

Lawmakers worry the AI could complicate an already strained system. In 2025, Duffy said the FAA was short 3,000 air traffic controllers.

“We ask that you pause any use of the SMART tool until we can better understand your decision-making, rollout process and evaluation plan,” the letter from Democrats continued, noting that safety workers have said they were not given an ample heads-up about the technology’s deployment.

The FAA said in an email to The Washington Sun that a team of specialists will analyze the data and provide scheduling recommendations to the agency’s Air Traffic Control System Command Center.

The recommendations will then be routed to air traffic control facilities for consideration by local leadership.

“As the agency continues to test SMART, train employees, and assess how the program is working, additional solutions will be rolled out,” the agency said.

In response to calls to suspend the technology’s use, Duffy wrote on X: “Here’s the truth: HUMANS still control the airspace and HUMANS still make the calls. With SMART, we are giving air traffic controllers new technology and better data to make critical decisions.”

Not all lawmakers oppose the technology. In a September statement, Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania) said the agencies are changing the industry from “reactive to predictive.”

He added: “I recognize how beneficial this tool and other investments will be for all our air traffic controllers.”

entries.title: Judge Clears the Name of a Top FEMA Official Fired by the Trump Administration
entries.summary: A federal judge laid into the Trump administration for spreading false information about the former FEMA official and exhibiting “outrageous government conduct.”
entries.content:
A federal judge on Tuesday formally cleared the name of a former high-level Federal Emergency Management Agency officer who faced a barrage of attacks from the Trump administration after her termination, citing “outrageous government conduct” perpetuated by top government officials.

The Department of Homeland Security fired Mary Comans, FEMA’s chief financial officer, on Feb. 11, 2025, but her termination notice did not list a cause. The same day, DHS issued a press release saying she had been fired “for circumventing leadership to unilaterally make egregious payments for luxury NYC hotels for migrants.”

High-ranking government officials, including Kristi Noem and Elon Musk, “engaged in a coordinated public relations campaign to impugn the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans,” U.S. Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick wrote. DHS officials also provided a statement to the press incriminating Comans for the alleged hotel scheme, which the department knew “was false at the time it was made,” he added.

Musk, who started leading the Department of Government Efficiency in January 2025, accused Comans of “criminal action” in a post on X on the day she was fired. And during her tenure as homeland security secretary, Noem provided information to far-right activist Laura Loomer, who made posts further denigrating Comans’ image.

Musk also reposted a picture of Comans, revealing the civil servant’s face to his millions of followers.

“Posting Ms. Comans’ picture served no legitimate governmental interest and was little more than state sanctioned intimidation,” Fitzpatrick, who presided over the name-clearing proceedings, wrote in his ruling.

The attacks on Comans “were based on the incorrect belief” that she had acted in violation of President Donald Trump’s January 2025 executive order that froze federal funding to non-governmental organizations that provide resources to undocumented immigrants, Fitzpatrick wrote.

The confusion over the hotel payments spurred from whether the order extended to pausing similar FEMA payments made to state and local governments. Comans continued to make tens of millions in payments to New York City's Office of Management and Budget for hotels for the immigrants after FEMA decided that payments should continue to be issued to state and local governments.

“This decision was explicitly approved by employees of the newly created Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) who were embedded with DHS and were reviewing and approving all funding initiatives,” Fitzpatrick wrote.

Comans filed two lawsuits against DHS, FEMA and the Executive Office of the President after her termination, arguing members of the Trump administration had knowingly defamed her using false statements and that she had been unlawfully terminated without due process.

In July, U.S. District Judge Michael Nachmanoff found that Comans had been unjustly fired. Nachmanoff ruled that Trump’s decision to unilaterally fire her under Article II of the Constitution ignored Comans’ right to review her termination through the Merit Systems Protection Board, which handles appeals for federal employees.

Nachmanoff’s decision did not reinstate Comans, and the Trump administration is actively appealing that ruling. But, in an unusual move, Nachmanoff ordered a formal name-clearing hearing for the former FEMA official — after which Fitzpatrick ruled in her favor to “correct the public record and establish as a matter of law that the statements made by these officials about Ms. Comans were objectively and demonstrably false.”

Trump has faced scrutiny for issuing several executive orders to bypass the traditional mechanisms for appeal for civil servants in the executive branch.

Comans isn’t the first government employee to challenge their termination. The Justice Department fired Maurene Comey, a senior federal prosecutor and the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, in July 2025. Like Comans, Comey filed a lawsuit challenging what she sees as an unconstitutional termination linked to Trump’s deeply held issues with her father.
